Thingol sat at the edge of the garden and watched as everything was taken out of his house. The chairs, the fluffy rug — the fluffy rug! — even his litter box. What were Oromë and Vána thinking? He rubbed his face in a flower, and then in the dirt. The smell was comforting. Soon enough, he was scooped up and stuffed into the horrible little box. He cried and cried, but no one listened. They just turned the music up louder. He was dropped in an empty house. At least it had big windows. Why was he here? Would he ever get back to the old garden? The stuff started to be brought back in. At least the fluffy rug would return. The door was open. Thingol ran.
Beyond the door was no garden. Instead, there was a forest, with trees so tall he could barely see the top of them. Thingol looked back at Oromë and Vána chattering away happily, and he darted into the woods. The air was cool and clear. It had so many smells he couldn't place, and he
loved it. Thingol ran and ran, farther and farther away from this new home that was not home. He was almost ready to turn back when he heard something. It sounded like a bird, and yet it was not a bird, he was certain. It was far sweeter. He followed it as if entranced, until he came upon the most beautiful cat he had ever seen. She was fluffy, with black stripes, and a deep gaze. She was the source of the sound! And just then, a bird flew right by her paw and she swatted it and bit into it. She pattered over to Thingol and dropped it at his feet — an offering. He just looked at her and started to purr. They stayed in the woods together for a long time.
She brought him food she had hunted and he was content to just be near her. Every night they watched the stars turning through the gaps in the trees. One day, a kitten was born to them, fluffy and warm. When he licked the kitten to clean her Thingol felt as though he had woken up from a long sleep, and he remembered Vána and Oromë, left all alone. He told Melian about them and convinced her to come with him back to meet them. They took turns carrying the kitten in their mouths — Lúthien was her name — with them and back to the door of the house, beyond the forest. They sat meowing at the door for some time. When Vána and Oromë saw them they let out a shriek of excitement and confusion. They came over and petted Thingol behind the ear, and Melian and Luthien as well, and Thingol was glad and content.

The ball room was a scene nothing short of modern elegance and wealth. Grand chandeliers glittered overhead, beautiful paintings from the most well known artist lined the walls, and the many nobles and their servants were dressed to match. A large stage at the front and center of the room tied everything together. It was dark outside but no one would have been able to tell with the lack of windows and the well lit room.
The nobles milled about, talking amongst themselves, and their servants remained silent at their side. This was one of the only times of celebration for the nobles so they took advantage of it. Some chatted formally about politics and other worldly matters, while some spoke excitedly of what was to come. The servants simply shared looks amongst each other, all of them with the same question in their eyes.
Once all of the nobles arrived, the room grew quiet and the lights dimmed. Everyone turned to face the stage, awaiting the appearance of their leader. And right on time as always, the man stepped out onto the stage. His signature mask covered his face, white with gold accents and covering all skin, just like the rest of his clothing. His steps were silent as he walked to the middle of the stage.
“Welcome! It is wonderful to see you all, my dear doves.” He greeted, his booming voice carrying across the room. Everyone bowed, just as they had their whole lives. “Let us all move along to what we have gathered here for.”
On queue, the bowl of hot stones was brought onto the stage from the left and the table was brought onto the stage from the right. The two women who brought the items onto stage met int the middle and set them down, the bowl was placed perfectly on the center of the table. With the items placed each woman took a single step back before going still. They would stand there until the ceremony was over, watching to make sure everything went smoothly.
With the stone ready, the masked man started to call names. “Acrilista.” With each name called, a servant left their nobles side and made their way to the stage, each step heavier than the last.
They all placed their right hand on the hot stones and held it there for two seconds. After, they would return to their noble, palm closed and eyes down cast. “Birlomere.” The only voice in the room was the man calling out names.
Soon enough, the thirty servants had gone to the stage, the stone had been shuffled thirty times, thirty names had been called. The lights began to brighten once more as the last servant returned to her noble’s side. “Let the divine mark be revealed.” The masked man called out and all of the servants raised their right hand.
It only took two seconds for the masked man to point at the servant with the mark. “Nevikalian.” He boomed and everyone turned to look at both the noble and the servant Lady Lambitari and Mr. Nevikalian. The rest of the servants lowered their hands, placing both of their hands behind their backs. The nobles clasped their hands together in front of them.
“Come to the stage.” The masked man commanded and Lady Lambitari and Mr. Nevikalian started to walk, the servant following behind the noble.
Lady Lambitari kneeled down in front of the table, facing the crowd. Mr. Nevikalian moved to stand in front of her, his back to the crowd. All eyes were on them as Lady Lambitari drew a dagger from the holster on her hip. It was a beautiful blade, reserved for an even more beautiful ceremony. The blade glimmered in the light as she held it up and bowed her head.
“Today, a sister joins the divine society above and a brother joins you in ruling our blessed land.” With that, Mr. Nevikalian takes the dagger by the handle and raises it, arms feeling as if they were made of lead.
He hesitated, eyes wide and heavy breathing. “Don’t let your mind be tainted by demons, brother. Follow your duty.” The masked man states, his voice deceivingly calm.
Mr. Nevikalian’s arms dropped and Lady Lambitari slumped to the ground. The blood pooled on the floor and the crowd cheered their names.

. . .The distinct smell of blood . . .

She hates it farther forward than that because she hates Misty, and she hates the hold that all of them have on her, and she hates that part of her life will always be trapped, lost and almost alone, begging for a home that barely even existed. She isn’t into the dusty marks on the ground or the bits of bone and brain matter scattered across bloodstains so dark they look like shadows at this hour. It doesn’t turn her on in any way to see evidence markers scattered all around behind shining yellow tape, like taping a package neatly shut. Not that she didn’t do her share of that, back when, but Taissa’s not thinking about that.Not thinking about long sleepless nights, pinching herself to stay awake, hearing every rustle and scuff of fabric, every soft wet sound, every stifled moan filling the hours when everyone was meant to be a sleep, and most of them were. Taissa always knew how Misty sounded quiet, and she’s being quiet now, just the same.There was a time when Taissa wanted to make her loud, too.It’s not particular to Misty, the way it wasn’t really particular to any of them, the way it couldn’t really be personal, out there, when Taissa had to keep the personal locked away behind masks behind masks. Taissa didn’t prepare a mask for this. She has them for ignoring violence, for grieving those who sicken her, for a gentle call to action in someone else’s words. At his idol with what has to be the most embarrassing expression someone’s ever made. Slack jawed. His eyes move over Robby’s aged face, down his faded and worn band tshirt, to his large hands as they move gracefully over the guitar strings.Fucking hell.Dennis’ breath catches when his eyes move back up, body going completely still.Robby stares back at him. She’d accidentally walked into a satyr convention in Central Park.

She’d even caught Hermes stealing her last slice of blue cheesecake—TWICE.
But nothing—absolutely nothing—prepared her for this.
She stared at Poseidon like he had just walked out of a reality show called Olympians Behaving Badly.
Poseidon, god of the sea, earthquakes, horses, and now apparently biological confusion, stared back at her with genuine hope shining in his ocean-green eyes.
And a little confusion.
Probably because Sally was blinking at him like he had actually grown a second head.
“Okay,” Sally finally said, raising a finger dramatically. “Let me see if I understood this correctly… You want to spend time with our baby—who is currently in my uterus—by using some kind of divine, oceanic, fish-adjacent magic to make you pregnant with him?”
Poseidon nodded brightly. “Exactly!”
“And this… aquatic transfer magic… would delay the birth until August?”
“Yes!” he replied, practically wagging his metaphorical tail.
Sally shut her eyes, took a deep breath, and rubbed the bridge of her nose.
Amphitrite, his immortal wife and Sally’s equally exasperated girlfriend, sighed deeply.She had already finished her second glass of wine and was contemplating a third.
“Amphy,” Sally said, turning to her. “Sweetheart. My love. My favorite oceanic goddess who has the patience of a kindergarten teacher after five espressos… Could you explain this again? Because as a mere mortal woman, what Seidon here just suggested—” she jabbed a thumb at him “—sounds physically impossible outside of Discovery Channel.”
Poseidon pouted.

“No promises,” Sally muttered. Poseidon hummed in agreement.
Amphitrite pinched the bridge of her own nose.
“Even though we have physical bodies resembling humans, we are, in fact, an entirely different species. Divine biology follows the rules of our domains.”
“Domains,” Sally repeated. “Yes. So because you two are water gods, your reproduction is…”
“Similar to seahorses,” Amphitrite said plainly.
Sally blinked.
Poseidon beamed proudly.
“Seahorses,” Sally echoed.
“Yes,” Amphitrite continued with the tone of someone explaining algebra to a clam. “The female transfers her unfertilized eggs into the male’s incubation pouch, where fertilization and development occur.”
Sally opened her mouth. Closed it. Opened it again.
Poseidon helpfully added, “I have a pouch!”
Sally pointed at him. “YOU DO NOT HAVE A POUCH.”
“I do! Not normally visible, but I can manifest one. Want to see?”
“NO!”
Sally threw both hands up.
Amphitrite sighed again. “Darling, focus.”
Sally took another breath.
“Okay. Seahorses.”
“Yes.”
“The female gives the male the eggs.”
“Yes.”
“And the male gets pregnant.”
“Correct.”
“So if I were a sea goddess, this would make sense.”
“Absolutely.” Amphitrite nodded.
“But I am not.”
“That is also correct.”

Poseidon raised a hand like an overeager student.
“Magic!”

“Seidon, sweetie,” Sally said gently, “mortals do not have transferable eggs. We don’t have divine, detachable, portable reproductive material.”

Sally stared.
Amphitrite drank.
“Sweet seaweed, he’s serious,” Sally whispered.
Poseidon lifted both hands. “I just thought—since you two can transfer your essence to me psychically—maybe you could also transfer the baby physically.”
“Psychic connection is not biology!” Amphitrite snapped.
Sally threw her head back. “I need to sit down.”
A wave of cushions floated up from nowhere and gently deposited her onto the couch. Perks of being in Poseidon’s domain.
Poseidon leaned forward, eyes big and hopeful. “I know it’s surprising, Sally. But could you maybe—possibly—give us your answer?”
“No pressure,” Amphitrite added.

Uzi opened her eyes to the obnoxious beeping of her alarm clock, gradually exiting sleep mode and reaching over to shut the alarm off. An intense throbbing in her head made itself known, her body not finding the strength to move just yet.
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 She stared up at the ceiling as she lay there, her thought process still waking up as well.
 
 
 
 
 After waiting a few more moments, Uzi finally managed to sit up, blinking hazily. She was hit with a strong wave of dizziness upon doing so, the room around her appearing to tilt.
 
 
 She glanced over at the clock, wanting to find out how much time was left before class started; However, she found herself unable to read the numbers as the gradual distortion in her vision grew.
 
 
 
 
 What in....
 
 
 
 
 Uzi placed a hand to her forehead with a groan as the pain worsened, forcing her to close her eyes again and lay back down.
 
 
 
 
 Ugh, what is this...?
 
 
 
 
 Despite closing her eyes, Uzi could still feel the dizzy sensation, along with an increase in her internal temperature.
 
 
 She breathed in and out heavily as the throbbing persisted, her thoughts becoming more and more difficult to process as she tried to figure out what was wrong with her.
 
 
 She wanted to call for help, however, she felt that doing so would make everything even worse. So, she just stayed there and suffered silently, hoping that whatever was screwing with her systems would clear up as soon as possible.

 When he was met with silence for about five long minutes, he knocked again in case she hadn't heard him the first time.
 
 
 
 
 More silence.
 
 
 
 
 Huh.
 
 
 
 
 N hesitated on whether or not he should try opening the door, not wanting to violate Uzi's privacy despite how uneasy her silence felt.
 
 
 
 
 Did I do something to upset her...? Is she ignoring me...?
 
 
 
 
 He tried to go through every possible and logical reason for Uzi's silence, but none of them really felt right.
 
 
 Eventually his concern won and he finally decided to try the door, which slid open with a whirr.
 
 
 
 
 Please forgive me for doing this, Uzi...
 
 
 
 
 He tensed, preparing to be scolded as he stepped into the room, but was met with darkness instead.
 
 
 
 
 Now he was hit with the sudden realisation that she may have slept in, and was, in fact, not even awake yet.
 
 
 
 
 "...Uzi?" he called quietly, activating his night vision briefly to focus in on her bed and confirm her presence from where he stood.
 
 
 
 
 Shortly after N had called her name, he was answered with a soft whimper. This sparked a sense of alarm in him, and he approached her, deactivating his night vision and turning on one of the dimmer lights in the room.
 
 
 
 
 "Uzi—What's wrong?" he asked with concern.
 
 
 
 
 Uzi didn't answer, only rolling over onto her side and curling up just partially on the bed. The tip of her tail twitched in a rhythmic manner, and the sound of her rapid artificial breathing filled the otherwise silent room.
 
 
 
 
 "Uzi," N called a bit louder, placing a hand on her shoulder. Instantly upon contact, he could feel the heat radiating from her body, and took notice of the occasional flash of a temperature warning on her visor.
 
 
 
 
 Concern started to turn into panic when she shuddered under his touch, beginning to mumble under her breath unintelligibly.
 
 
 
 
 "H-Hey, can you hear me?" N asked in one last attempt at getting a direct response from her.
 
 
 
 
 "...Uhhhhhhhhhhuh...." Uzi finally groaned in answer, opening her heterochromatic eyes just barely to look up at N with an unfocused gaze.
 
 
 
 
 N sighed in relief upon receiving a more direct answer. Unfortunately, that relief quickly faded when Uzi started rambling again.
 
 
 
 
 "Why won't...shhhh...she would...."
 
 
 
 
 "...U-Uzi, I'm...not sure what that means," N stated nervously.

The garden was quiet in that soft, forgotten way—overgrown, uneven, touched by time. Ivy climbed the pillars like old memories, and flowers spilled out of their beds, brushing her skirts as she walked. Even the sunlight came in gently here, filtered through arches and leaves.This was where they sent her—to calm herself, to think, to prepare—on the night before the engagement ceremony.Yoon I-rang stood in the center of the cloister, hands folded, back straight. Even alone, she held herself like someone was watching. Grace had been trained into her so deeply it felt like a second spine. She had learned early to speak only when spoken to, to keep her voice soft, her smile smaller than her thoughts.She wasn’t born to be ordinary.She was born to be queen.The fifth in her line to inherit the title, I-rang had never imagined another life. Her ancestors wrote history; she was expected to continue it. The Crown Prince was her match—intelligent, refined, chosen by tradition and timing. Their union had been planned before she could write her name. She accepted it like a duty: to protect the throne, even if it meant sacrificing parts of herself.But even queens, sometimes, look back.“You’re here,” a voice said behind her.She didn’t turn immediately. His presence always changed the air—lighter, warmer, somehow more honest. Still, she glanced over her shoulder.Prince LeeAhn—Lee Wan—stood a few steps away. He wasn’t wearing royal attire, just an ivory suit that made him look strangely human, almost out of place. Less like a prince, more like a man trying not to be one.“The Crown Prince wanted to be alone,” he said. “So they sent me to see if his bride-to-be needed anything.”I-rang met his gaze. “Did you come as his shadow, or yourself?”A faint twist of his lips. Not quite a smile. “Does it matter?”“It does,” she said, turning toward him. “Shadows don’t speak like this.”He took a small step closer—slow, careful. “And queens don’t answer so directly.”Silence settled between them, long enough to hear the wind move through the flowers.Her breath tightened. He was close enough that if she closed her eyes, she could still remember the warmth of his hands on her waist, the taste of the rain the night he kissed her beneath the moon. Memories she had buried for the crown, but not deeply enough.“You shouldn’t be here,” she whispered.“I know.”“You shouldn’t look at me like that.”His eyes stayed on hers. “I know that, too.”This was the rebellion they never dared to name. They had simply been in love. Before the throne intervened. Before the elders reminded her of her duty. Before she realized that a future queen could not bind herself to the prince who had nothing to offer the crown.Before she chose ambition over him.Before she broke his heart to secure her own future.He looked at her now the way he always had—like she was the only thing in the world that ever made sense.And maybe because he saw her—not the crown, not the duty, but I-rang.The girl he once watched running barefoot in the rain.The girl no one else remembered.She didn’t know whether to hate him for that, or cling to it.“Is it hard?” he asked softly. “Carrying everything?”“No,” she said after a moment. “It gets heavier when you try to set it down.”His eyes lowered, just for a second. As if he understood too well. As if he wished he didn’t.“Do you wish it was me?” he asked quietly, the words almost inaudible.The words hit I-rang like a breath caught in her chest. She froze. Not because it wasn't trueㅡbecause it was.Yes.It had always been him.But fate is never gentle with those who ask for more than what it offers.She didn’t answer. A queen can’t.She walked past him, steady and poised, toward the arches where brighter light waited. Every step pulled her back into the role she had been born for. Her silence was the only reply she could give—and it held more than any words.Lee Wan didn’t follow. He stayed where he was, watching her leave, hands clenched loosely at his sides as if holding back something he had never been allowed to reach for.And in that old garden—built for reflection, soaked in unspoken truths—they left behind the one thing neither of them could say:
Sometimes the heart chooses its own ruler.And sometimes it chooses wrong.

Little Red Riding Hood, or Rose since that was her actual name, was just strolling through the woods. After what the hunter had shown her, she had never feared the woods again. She was actually just a baker now, something simple and fun. Her grandma had taught her how to bake before the whole getting eaten by a wolf thing. Needless to say, Rose was doing well for herself!The three little pigs were not. John, Jake, a Jonathan were not having a good time. They had never had a good time considering their parents decided to cop out on the youngest's name, but today was particularly bad. John and Jake were booking it from Jake's stick house, or his pile of sticks at this point, to Johnathan's brick house. They told him it was far to expensive to make, but maybe they should've been a little less dumb, or that's what Johnathan would say."Hey- Hey! You can't just run into me like that!" Rose snapped. The two pigs went tumbling. They tried to scramble to their feet as fast as they could, and Jake was successful. Unfortunately, John was closer to Rose and the back of his tail coat was stepped on."You don't understand, Miss! There's a wild wolf after us! He blew our houses down!" John panicked. Rose looked behind her, the unmistakable shimmer of yellow eyes in the distance. She took her foot off of John's tailcoat and grabbed her hatchet."He blew your houses down, you say? What, were they made of hay and twigs?"They weren't going to answer that…"Don't worry. I know a thing or two about wolves," Rose assured. She let the wolf come closer, hiding the hatchet behind her back. She whistled as wolf snarled, circling his prey."Well, well, well… Three whole pieces of meat for my liking! Why don't we-" Before he could finish, the wolf had stepped in front of Rose, giving her the perfect opportunity to swing her axe directly into his stomach. She hacked at him a couple times, maybe her own trauma sending her into overdrive, but the wolf was very much dying by the time she was done with him."That was easy! I thought wolves knew woman were too smart to prey on. Then again, you were chasing those idiots over there… Well, it's the end of the line for you! Say goodbye big…  bad… wolf," Rose trailed off. She raised her hatchet above her head and sent it crashing down onto the wolf's skull in one, singular motion.Well, he was definitely dead now."Now, scramble along. I have places to be and a dress to clean," Rose dismissed. She walked off, stepping over the body of the wolf as she went. John and Jake were stunned. They hadn't been expecting that of all things. However, they did take Rose's advice and scramble out of there as fast as they could. Johnathan was not going to believe a word out of their mouths for the next hour.

The first time you meet, he says something mundane like "nice to meet you." Which isn't wrong. It is nice to meet you. And you seem nice. More than nice, really, with a friendly grin the hides the loneliness you must feel after uprooting yourself to a new town.Alex knows how daunting that can be.New faces. A new home. Not knowing the layout. He thinks maybe he could show you around, but before he can offer, Sam shows up on his skateboard with his easy charm and wide grin. He says a reluctant goodbye, hoping to meet again.He sees you again the next day. He talks about being the all-star quarterback in high school, even though he graduated a couple of years ago. He could kick himself for bringing up his old glory, hoping he doesn't sound like he's bragging.To his surprise, you seem genuinely interested, asking about stats and his favourite team. He's thrilled to learn you like the Tunnellers, too, and debates if he should invite you to watch the game together.But his television is small, and Grandpa would be there. Not that he's embarrassed, but Grandpa can be prickly. Maybe another time.At the Flower Dance, you come up to him right away, your eyes so full of hope, it almost feels cruel to say no. But he promised to dance with Haley, as he always did. There had never been another option until this year.As he spins Haley around, he keeps his eye on you, his stomach sinking as you try to discreetly wipe away a tear. He wants a re-do. Maybe he could even ask you for the next dance, but then Lewis announces the Flower Court winners and he has to pose for endless pictures. Maybe next year.Over time, he opens up to you. He finds himself telling you about almost everything: why he lives with his grandparents, his struggles with reading, his hidden hopes and dreams.He apologizes for being rude when you first met, but you look surprised. He's equally surprised when you tell him you didn't think he was rude. A little overconfident, maybe, but you're smiling as you say it and that makes him feel better.He tells you almost everything, but he still holds back. You can tell. Perhaps in a little while, he'll share it all.You find him on the beach, his music box tucked in his hand. He tells you about his mom, how much he loves her and misses her. He tries to hide his tears, but you put your arm around him and he buries his head in your shoulder.You tell him you'll always be there for him, and for the first time in years, he allows himself to dream about something other than gridball. A future that seems both within reach and so far away. An echo of unconditional love that reminds him of home. Familiar yet different. The music fades and you say farewell.Alex shifts in his bed, blinking against the light of the early morning sun filtering through the crack in his blind. It's rare that he sleeps long enough to have the sun wake him. Even in summer, he is up before dawn, anxious to begin his daily routine.For a moment, he's confused by the colours on his bedside table, his sleep-addled brain trying to figure out what, exactly, he's looking at, when a flurry of memories from the night before rush in all at once.A question asked in between stammers. His heart beating as he gave his answer, sealing it with a slow kiss. Fingers running through his hair as he pulled his farmer - pulled you - closer to him, his body slotting into place alongside yours as if they were made to fit together. Trading breaths. Trading heartbeats. All merging into one until the rustle of a passing rabbit startled him and the two of you hastily broke apart.Then a giggle and another lingering kiss and a 'see you soon.' Not goodbye. Just… until next time.Alex runs his finger along the soft petals of the flowers. He smiles as he repeats his promise: "until next time."Another question soon follows. Water drips down your hair as you try to catch your breath, having run to him directly from the beach.
Water pools around your feet and Alex vows to clean it up so Granny doesn't slip and fall.
Later.
Right now all he can do is say yes. He picks you up and spins you around, before your lips meet again. He feels happiness. He hasn't felt this happy for years. At one point, he wondered if he'd ever be happy again. He pinches himself to make sure this is real.
It is.Three more days.He grins nervously as you walk down the aisle. You've never looked more breathtaking and Alex can barely concentrate on the words Lewis is saying.Until he hears you say 'I do.''I do," he replies, almost too quickly. A hint of a laugh passes through the crowd, but he's too busy wiping the tears of happiness off your cheeks to notice. You wipe his off, too.A song plays over the loudspeaker and he begins to cry harder, but you don't seem to mind. You kiss him as the music box's melody plays a promise of endless tomorrows. Together.

"I need you to tell me it's okay, Sammy." The waver in Dean's voice echoes the tremble in Sam's hand when he strokes Dean's hair and shushes him."It's alright, Dean," Sam says soothingly--distracting him as he pulls a knife from his belt. Dean sees it anyway, of course, and tries to shake his head, tries to speak when Sam wraps their hands around the handle together, but all that comes out is a quiet moan.Sam quiets him again, makes sure the point is centered between his ribs--then hesitates. Dean's head is drooping when Sam pulls out his cell phone and tosses it into a nearby pile of hay."Call 9-1-1," he says clearly, loudly enough that Dean manages to lift his head from Sam's shoulder."Please, Sammy." Barely a whisper, and Sam would give him this if he could--but he can't. He won't. Not this time."I can't do this without you, Dean. And I don't want to."He tilts Dean's head back against the post gently and slides the hand not holding the knife around Dean's shoulders. Rapidly cooling wetness soaks his sleeve but he doesn't care, not now. A soft kiss--first, last--and "I love you so much, big brother" as the blade sinks home.The darkness only lasts for a moment, Sam thinks, though it's not like he would know. When he opens his eyes Dean is still in his arms, lips still pressed together, exactly as they were. He starts to step back, to look around, to see heaven, but Dean's arms tighten around him, keeping him close. It's not until his scalp tingles and stings that he realizes Dean has one hand in his hair, that Dean's kissing him. He melts against his brother, the joy inside him matched by Dean's as their souls touch for the first time since before Dean was born.Sam has no idea how long it lasts, content to stay here forever if Dean wants to, just like this, but the sound of a throat being loudly cleared eventually breaks the silence. Dean startles back, and they realize at the same time that they're standing in front of an old, familiar shack. There's three rocking chairs on the porch, one of them occupied by Bobby, who's currently digging around in a familiar green cooler.Sam steps forward first. "Bobby?" he says, uncertainty making him hesitant because there's no doubt their old friend saw what he saw. But Bobby just grunts, holding out two icy, dripping bottles, not meeting their eyes as they climb the rickety steps.Bobby doesn't speak until they're both seated, until they've all taken a long, cold drink."Well," he says eventually. "Scarred for life takes on a whole new meaning when you can't die."Dean flushes bright red, but he doesn't apologize so Sam doesn't either. "It's heaven," he says, shrugging, and Bobby heaves a longsuffering sigh."We've all been waiting for you," he says eventually, letting it go. He still doesn't meet their eyes but Sam's grateful, doesn't want him to see the sparkle of the unfallen tears summoned by Bobby's acceptance and love."John and Mary've got a place over there--" his beer bottle tilts vaguely north--"and Castiel's around here somewhere, though you probably won't recognize him. Angels don't wear meat suits in heaven." He studies the horizon for a moment, carefully not looking at either of them. "You idjits gonna head over?"Before Sam can answer, Dean shakes his head, a smile lighting up his eyes as he nods toward where Baby has suddenly always been, her chrome gleaming in the afternoon sun. Sam smiles with him, knowing what he's gonna say. "Nah. I think we'll just go for a drive."

Chapter 1: An Unexpected Request
Harry Potter stood on the balcony of Peverell Castle, watching the Tuscan sun paint the rolling hills in shades of amber and gold. A glass of wine—a habit he'd picked up since moving to Italy—dangled loosely from his fingers. At twenty-three, he'd finally found peace, far from the demands of a wizarding Britain that wanted him to be their saviour, their poster boy, and apparently, Ginny Weasley's husband.
The wards chimed softly, announcing the arrival of a visitor. Harry's jaw tightened. Only a handful of people knew how to find him, and he wasn't expecting anyone to come.
He made his way through the castle's ancient corridors, his footsteps echoing off stone that had stood for over a thousand years. When he opened the heavy oak door, the last person he expected to see was Severus Snape.
"Snape." Harry blinked, taking in the man before him. Severus looked different than he had during the war—still pale, still dressed in black, but there was a softness around his eyes that hadn't existed before. The scar on his neck, courtesy of Nagini, was barely visible beneath a high collar.
"Potter." Severus's lips quirked in what might have been amusement. "You look well. Italy agrees with you."
"I—thank you?" Harry stepped aside automatically. "How did you—never mind. Come in. Would you like some tea? Coffee? Wine?"
"Wine, actually. Thank you."
They settled in Harry's favorite sitting room, the one with floor-to-ceiling windows overlooking the vineyards. Harry poured them both generous glasses of Chianti.
"I imagine you're wondering why I'm here," Severus said after a long sip.
"The thought crossed my mind."
"I need your help with something... delicate."
Harry raised an eyebrow. "Delicate?"
Severus sighed, setting down his glass. "Do you remember Lucius Malfoy?"
"Hard to forget him." Harry's voice went carefully neutral. "What about him?"
"He's..." Severus paused, seeming to search for words. "He's trying to rebuild his life. After the trials, after Azkaban, after losing everything. He's genuinely changed, Harry."
"That's good for him." Harry took a drink, wondering where this was going.
"He's asked for my help with something, and I—" Severus looked almost embarrassed. "I'm not the right person for this. But you are."
"Severus, what exactly did Lucius Malfoy ask you for?"
"Cooking lessons."
Harry choked on his wine. "I'm sorry, what?"
"Cooking lessons. Proper ones. Lucius has realised that he knows nothing about caring for himself without house-elves, without servants, without his wife." Severus's expression was serious. "He wants to learn to cook. And I told him I knew someone who could help."
"Why would you think of me?"
"Because you grew up cooking for the Dursleys. Because you've been living independently here, clearly thriving. Because you know what it's like to have to learn everything from nothing." Severus leaned forward. "And because, despite everything, you're one of the few people who might give him a genuine chance at redemption."
Harry stared at his former professor. "You want me to teach Lucius Malfoy how to cook."
"Yes."
"Here. In Italy."
"Ideally, yes. He needs to be away from England, away from the judgmental eyes and the gossip. And you need..." Severus gestured vaguely. "You've been hiding, Harry. Perhaps it's time to live again."
Harry wanted to argue, but the words caught in his throat. Severus wasn't wrong. He'd been hiding. Running, really, from Hermione's disappointed looks when he refused her matchmaking attempts, from Ron's confusion at Harry's lack of interest in Ginny, from Molly's tears and Arthur's gentle suggestions that "Dumbledore knew best."
"This is insane," Harry said finally.
"Most worthwhile things are." Severus stood. "Think about it. I'll return in three days for your answer."
After Severus left, Harry stood on his balcony again, watching the stars emerge over the Italian countryside. Lucius Malfoy. Here. Learning to cook.
It was absolutely mad.
Which was probably why Harry was already considering it.

I'll breathe your air for a moment. I’ll still reach out and feel the empty space you’ve left. I’ll take the small interactions we have while patrolling.
But really, I want to take your hand into mine. Feel your body heat in my palm. Let it linger and spread up my arm and throughout my chest. I’ll become delusional. And that’s fine, as long as I can still see your eyes.
Aki. You have no idea. I’ll
I’ll watch you sleep and imagine myself next to you. And that’s what I did.
I was currently staying the night at Aki’s apartment. Denji and Power were already passed out in their shared room, probably sweating from this summer heat. I sat at the coffee table with my elbows propped up on the edge. A grayish blue hue soaked the living room, and a humid breeze pushed through the open window.
Aki lay on the floor with a single pillow cushioned under his head.
“You don’t have to stay out here ya know” I said, tucking my feet under me. We just got done cleaning up after dinner. The TV was playing a game show but i wasn't paying much attention to it.He could have gone to his room and slept comfortably in his bed. But I’m also happy he didn’t. I can selfishly watch his chest rise and fall as he dreams about whatever.“I’m not tired yet. You’re also a guest; I can’t just leave you out here bored and alone.” He said planting himself across from me, facing the TV.
Alone. I would’ve been fine with that. I have been fine with it. Then I met you.
I push away from the coffee table and crawl quietly to where he is. One hand up above his head, the other tucked in under his shirt lying flat on his stomach, exposing just a sliver of skin. I hang above him and watch his subtle breaths, in and out. His lashes are so dark and thick yet short. Eyebrows that usually furrowed in deep thought are now relaxed in sleep. Peach fuzz covers his cheeks and jaw. I move my hand just above his face, inches away. I can feel his breath on my palm, so light and calm. I make shadows along his hairline and think about pushing the strands away from his forehead.
I trace the space above his skin and make a small circle.‘Right there, Aki. That’s where I’d kiss you.’I lean just a little and he starts to stir.
‘This was so stupid. Fuck.’
I push myself away, but his hand raises, floating for a second before he moves it towards my face.I look down and his dark blue eyes are open and groggy. Just a small light reflecting from the patio, soft and yellow. I can see a faint blush on the tops of his cheeks.His hand maneuvers around my head and along my neck before he lands on my lips. Inches away as always.
“I’d kiss you here, Angel.”
He smiles and lets his hand fall as he turns over, facing the patio door.
Panting, I stand up and speed walk to the bathroom, shoving my wings in with me.
I look up into the mirror.Here.My lips on his.
Was that Aki reciprocating? He said my name so maybe? I’m sweating now and it’s not from the summer swelter that’s happening. Heat rises to my cheeks and up my neck all to the tips of my ears.
‘This is embarrassing. Why am I even here?’
I turn the faucet on to splash water on my face, but I pause right before I do.
I can feel his hand almost touching my face and his warmth. His smile and blush on his gentle tired face.
I turn the faucet off and walk out with a dry face.
I return to my original spot at the table and lie on the back on the cool floor. Wings splayed out.
I finally fall asleep listening to Aki softly snoring.
“Good morning, peasants!” Power says after a very restful night. Well for her anyway.
“What you got cooking, Aki?” Denji is leaning over Aki’s shoulder and looking in a pan of fried eggs. Aki gives him a nudge to the rib and hands him a plate.
“I’m almost done, make your ‘toast’ while I finish,” he says as cracks another egg into the pan. “Angel and I have patrol in an hour, Power and Denji, I need you to be ready by that time so we can all leave together, ‘kay?”
I sit silent at the coffee table with my breakfast. Just an egg and toast. But I can still feel my stomach flipping from last night.
“I’d kiss you here, Angel.”
I shut my eyes tight and shake my head as if to have the memory fall out of my ears.
“You okay? I knew I shouldn’t have left that door open, too many bugs in the summertime.” Aki said as he sat himself down across from me on the floor.
He starts eating silently and I just watch. His jaw moving as he chews and Adam's apple bobbing with every sip of his coffee. Seeing him like this doesn’t feel right. Like I’m not allowed to see him after last night. I’m not allowed to see him so comfortable and domestic.
The light pours in from the sunrise, and he is engulfed in a brilliant glow. He looks more like an Angel right now than me. Loose messy hairs sit on his head as he sleepily finishes his breakfast, and I can’t stop staring. Until he starts speaking to me and I don’t realize it.“Hey, you better eat or else Denji with snatch it from you.” He says with a smirk and sips the last of his coffee.God. No one else

Shock. Fury. His silhouette streaked across the cavern wall, leaping from jutting stone to thick tendon-like protrusions along the bourgeon’s shell. Its mouth gaped impossibly wide, searching for another person to take from her.Lune planted her feet, ignoring the scream from her heels, and pulled breath into her lungs like she could force it to behave. Her next stain tore down her forearm like a hot blade. Searing pain flared so bright it fuzzed her edges, and for a heartbeat she was sure she’d tear something critical inside herself. Her breath hitched as she forced fire into the air with a violent exhale. The gout of flame slammed into the creature’s flank caused the bourgeon to jerk back but the blast barely charred the thick carapace.She was pushing too hard. Too fast. Breath came ragged and sharp with the echo of what she knew couldn’t be endured much longer.Normally she could counteract this sort of feedback by healing the injuries as soon they arrive but there wasn’t time to spend chroma on something so frivolous – not if she wanted to hold the beast at bay while Verso found a way out.“You okay down there?” Monoco called, voice going over the creature’s rumbling.She ignored him as its bulk shifted, each movement pounding waves through the ground. Fire and frost were sent striking against its shell again as rivets of her blood fall to the floor.What if this wasn’t just another reckless stunt from Verso that could be laughed at with relief masquerading as exasperation later? What if his vulnerability had a limit? What if he actually died this time?Her chest heaved, sweat stinging her eyes. She had to get to Verso. She had to keep Monoco from getting swallowed too. Sieun had pointedly ignored that little comment. Even though his gaze lingered on his mitt a little longer after that conversation. Constantly suffocated by never meeting his mother’s expectations and his father forever resenting him for giving up the one thing that drew them together. Baseball was supposed to be a silly little hobby anyways. A way to quiet his brain and provide a much needed distraction from the constant textbooks. Sieun wasn’t supposed to like it as much as he had.
He agreed to applying to Stanford at the very last second. Just in case none of the other schools wanted him.
“Sieun-ah, I sent our team a tape I clipped together from your senior year of high school. Coach said he would look it over and email you once he’s made up his mind. Check your inbox!”
That was two days ago. Juntae had emailed him on the coach’s behalf yesterday.
Sieun hasn’t checked it yet.
He doesn’t know what’s worse. Denial or a walk on offer. He doesn’t know which one he wants.

The restraints tighten around Noriko’s forearms. The execution chamber is dead silent, save for the sound of her own quickening breathing.She’s only so scared because she doesn’t know exactly how this will go down, Noriko reasons, just that it will end in death. This information, strangely, serves to bring her some speck of melancholic acceptance. There will be no surprise. There is no hope to be crushed.The air in the car is getting stuffier, Noriko notices. Is this really how she will die? How long will this take—hours? Days?Noriko, out of the very corner of her eye, can see the observation window, though she’s unable to see out the other side. One-way glass. She realizes that she’s thankful for this. Although Noriko would love to see Hidemi during her last moments, she couldn’t bear to watch her beg and cry hysterically, just like Noriko had watched Ruka. That would hurt more than any punishment the rabbit could bestow upon her.She recalls being on the other side of that glass, watching Nanae fruitlessly kick and punch and scratch at the unstoppable force of the walls until her knuckles bled. She remembers how her heart had sped up, as if she were in her place; as if she were the one who was about to meet her end.She is in Nanae’s place now, and she could almost laugh at how wrong she was. That feeling and this feeling are nothing alike. Half an hour ago, she would have never been able to comprehend something so visceral.Just then, her nose is filled with the scent of gasoline. She sniffs again in confirmation. She looks around as much as she can manage with her limited head movement, peering down at her feet when she notices something wet seeping into her shoes and socks. There is gasoline. A layer on the floor of the car. Has it always been here?No, no. It’s rising. It’s creeping upwards, to her ankles now.Noriko’s gut twists with fear—more than it already has, somehow.A searing headache hits full swing as she takes another breath. Noriko kicks her feet as much as she can with the restraints around her shins, as if it will save her. And yet, she tries to remain visibly calm. For Hidemi. She can see her. Noriko has to remember that. She’ll do anything to soften the blow—anything that’ll make this easier for Hidemi to stomach.Her emotions cycle through rage, panic, and guilt. She’s furious at the other members of the Bleeding, at the fact that there would still be a chance if not for their constant slip-ups, there had to be.She panics as she realizes that this is really the end. That she’s really going to die. That she’ll never go home, jumping into her worried sick parents’ arms. That she’ll never send an e-mail to Hidemi, or see Daiki walk freely.And she feels guilt for Mutsuko, that her fiery spirit was taken from this world as a sacrifice, all for it to be in vain. That she couldn’t save Taku, and that she couldn’t save Daiki and Hidemi. Was there ever a chance?The headache drills deeper into her skull. Her vision is growing spotty with oil spill-like dots.The gasoline is only at her knees, beginning to seep into the seat of the car. There’s still room to escape, Noriko thinks foolishly, only for a moment to make herself feel better. She makes no actual effort. She’s growing quite sluggish, actually.Noriko closes her eyes.Then it all hits at once again—her heart is beating too fast. She’s gasping for air at this point. She gains a sudden burst of adrenaline, thrashing in the seat of the car.The car is filling up faster. It’s over the cut on her stomach now.Noriko tries and tries to be calm, to think of nice things, the things that will fill anyone with a sense of serenity like waterfalls and flower fields, but she just can’t. She’s suddenly very present, and she can only focus on what’s happening at this very moment. She wouldn’t be sure if she’s even breathing anymore if not for the sound of her gasps.Noriko has to stay strong for Hidemi. She has to. She has to escape, no matter how weak and powerless she feels. That’s always how it’s been.But she’s getting weaker again. This time, she knows her vigor isn’t coming back—and it never will. The gasoline reaches the choker around her neck. She tries to breathe as hard as she can.Noriko tilts her head up as far as it will go, knowing that she’s only delaying the inevitable.Noriko takes one final gasp, holding her breath as the gasoline creeps up to cover her nose.

Just because an individual has a broad understanding of certain subjects does not mean that they are knowledgeable in living. I had spent many years studying medicine so I could help people, and I spent even more time studying people. I grew up with no siblings, no friends, and only one parent who rarely left the temple on the head of the mountain at my home in Tibet. I raised myself, and because of that, I found it very hard to understand others, and yet I was curious and wanted to meet new people. That's why I became a doctor, so I could help others and learn to understand them. When your father came into my life, it was like everything I had worked for led up to that moment. And then you were born, and yet again I felt a burning need to protect and ensure your happiness. My son, I wish I could have known you for longer then the short amount of time we spent together. My biggest wish is to spend even just one day with you and your father again, doing things that a normal family would do. I hope that one day, you can feel that kind of peace. Even if its just a little bit, a fleeting pleasure that passes with the autumn breeze. I hope one day you know what it's like to love someone, to care for someone so much that your own wants and needs become second to theirs. I couldn't even manage to do that one thing that a mother should be able to do. You cried very rarely and I found this odd. The months grew colder, In Tibet, the winters are unbearably cold, especially for a weak baby like you. My son, you might be wondering why I'm writing all of this down, but it's because I don't want you to be left in the dark your whole life. Your father's family is close to finding out about us and my own clan in Tibet…has decided to make me a human sacrifice. It is now mere hours before they will drag me up to the mountain. My dear son, you are so little right now, but I already now that you be a great man. I will do everything I can to ensure that we can see each other again in the future, even if it means crawling back to you and your father until my nails are bleeding and have fallen off. Death feels nothing like Harry expected.No pain. No shock. No fear.
Just a lightness—an opening—like stepping out of a long, dim hallway into fresh air.And then the whiteness gathers around him.
Familiar.He knows the place before it forms.King’s Cross.Not exactly, but close enough that the soul recognises what the eyes do not. He stands there again, older now, aware, calm. The last time he was here, he was seventeen and afraid. This time he understands what it means.He also understands why he’s been brought back.There is someone else here.Harry walks through the mist. The silence isn’t silent; it is gentle, like waiting breath. And as he approaches, he sees the shape huddled on the ground, small and shuddering.The same shape he saw all those years ago.Still trapped.
Still unable to move.
Still suffering.Harry stops a few feet away.The thing that was Voldemort is curled on itself, twisted in pain that has no end. It does not look at him—he doubts it can. But he feels the echo of what it once was. The malice is gone; there is nothing left strong enough to hate him. Just a wounded scrap of a soul stuck in eternal stasis.For a long moment, Harry simply watches.He expected anger.
He expected revulsion.
He expected something darker.But all he feels is… pity.No one deserves this.
Not even Voldemort.He kneels—because in this place, intention shapes form—and he speaks softly.“You don’t have to stay here, Tom.”The thing trembles. It can’t understand him, not really. But his voice reaches it. Something in the fragment quivers like a needle toward a magnet.Harry extends a hand.The creature cannot take it—he knows that now—but the gesture matters. It gives the fragment something it hasn’t had since the moment of its creation:Direction. Permission. A path forward.Slowly, as if pulled by gravity, the small, ruined soul shifts toward him.Together, they rise.The station forms fully around them as they walk. Empty, clean, washed in mist. The train waits the way it did before, warm light spilling from the open door.Harry places a steadying hand on the misshapen back—not out of affection, but out of compassion. The fragment responds to the touch like a frightened child who doesn’t know what comfort is.“Come on,” he murmurs. “It’s time.”Voldemort steps onto the train.Immediately, Harry feels the shift.
A pull.
A judgement.
Something vast turning its attention.He doesn’t see what happens, not directly. The carriage fills with light, and the light pulls the fragment away—toward what lies beyond, toward whatever fate awaits the sum of Tom Riddle’s choices.It is over quickly.When the brightness fades, the carriage is empty.Harry stands alone on the platform.He feels no guilt. No triumph. Only the sense that something unfinished has finally been resolved. The tension of a cord that has been taut for decades now quietly lifts.He had not forgiven Voldemort.
But he had refused to let him suffer pointlessly.There is a difference.A soft presence appears at Harry’s side—Dumbledore, or the memory of him. Harry does not turn. He doesn’t need to.“Well done, Harry.”
The voice is warm. “You showed mercy where none was owed. That is a very rare thing.”Harry breathes in the mist, steady and peaceful.He steps onto the train.
The door closes gently behind him.
The platform dissolves.And Harry goes where he is meant to go.

Once she had safely borne an heir, then she might chance it.Her plan was all well and good, until the morning she stumbled upon a corpse in the pond.
Swans glided in serene ripples, wind rustled the willow boughs, and mud smeared her muslin skirts as she fell back from the horrific sight. In the end, Narcissa picked herself up from the mud and strode towards the manor with as much dignity as her shaky poise allowed. Past the wild shrubs that spilled into the lawn, she followed the path that ended at her mother-in-law’s garden. At the gate, she called for a house-elf.
After a moment that stretched on for so long, she wondered if they had all dropped dead, an elf finally appeared. No apology was offered for the delay, nor for the distracted curtsy she received.The lack of respect irked her. Narcissa possessed as much authority as any Malfoy, although no one seemed to remember that—not the house-elves anxious to return to their duties, and certainly not the brutes infesting their estate. The footsoldiers Lucius commanded did their best to make her life miserable. All week, they had laughed so uproariously underneath the windows that she’d found it impossible to read. She would have stormed outside and demanded they quiet down, but had decided to spare herself the humiliation of being ignored. Instead, she’d moved her reading to the pond underneath the willow tree, where nothing broke her peace but the gentle chirping of the birds overhead. Nothing, that was, until a rotting corpse had ruined that for her too.“You will accompany me to the pond,” she told the house-elf.The look of dismay that crossed its wrinkled face would have earned a Crucio from anyone else, but Narcissa only pursed her lips and trudged back through the garden. The reluctant house-elf followed.
After a silent journey across the lawn, they slowed to a halt at the edge of the bank. The corpse was just as she’d left it: bloated skin, bulging eyes, and tattered shirt tangled in the reeds. She hastily averted her gaze before the toast she’d had for breakfast could spill across the grass. The lack of reaction from the elf did not bode well for the prospect of her sanity.
“Do you see anything?”
“Yes, Mistress.”“Well, what do you see?” she snapped, unwilling to speak of her grotesque hallucinations to a servant. Word might get back to the household, and then Lucius would realise he had married a lunatic.“Henny sees a Muggle floating in the pond.”“You do?” She was so relieved, she could cry.

Where will I read now?”The pond had been her last bastion of tranquillity. She could flee to the library, but even among the rows of ancient tomes, a scream might shatter the dusty silence.
No matter. Lucius would have the men clean up the pond, and then she would return to her tainted sanctuary. What was a dead Muggle or two when one lived amongst a horde of Death Eaters? It was a marvel she hadn’t stumbled across worse.She turned her back on the grisly sight and walked along the footpath back to the manor, where men were milling about the terrace in the distance. Fortunately for her nerves, they seemed to be taking a break from hurling fiery flashes of magic at each other. She had no wish to be caught in a training accident so soon after her fright.

Game nights at Clint’s apartment weren’t anything official. They were mostly a ‘get away from the Tower/responsibilities/Avengers-related bullshit and blow off some steam’ kind of deal. Bucky found it quietly interesting to see which people preferred which kinds of games. When it was just him and Clint, usually they’d play first person shooters. Steve was a big fan of competitive co-op games, Natasha liked strategy RPGs, and Tony tended towards what he and Clint both dubbed ‘the classics’ aka older games that were easy to learn but hard to master.Bucky wasn’t sure how many times he’d driven his car off this stupid track, but it was getting pretty ridiculous at this point.“Don’t you dare blueshell me, you-!”The knock on the door was barely audible over the sound of Tony’s cursing and Clint’s gleeful victory. But Clint and Bucky were not-quite-ex spy/assassins and Tony was a paranoid bastard, so even with how quiet the knock at the door was, it didn’t go unnoticed by any of them.“You expecting someone else?”“Nah,” Clint said, moving to the door more casually than Bucky would’ve if someone unknown was knocking on his own door. “Probably just a resident, sorry, should just be a min-”He cut himself off as he opened the door. Presumably not a resident, then.“Hawkeye.”“Javelynn.”The tension in Clint’s voice had both Tony and Bucky leaning forward in their seats, ready to step in should it become necessary.“What are you doing here?”“Didn’t know where else to go.”The woman in the doorway coughed and swayed forward. Clint caught her instinctively.“Shit, what- One of you get the first aid kit. Now.”Clint had a couple first aid kits stashed around his place, but the one in the kitchen was closest so Bucky grabbed that one while Tony helped Clint maneuver the woman inside and lay her down on the couch. He winced in sympathy as her shirt rode up to reveal a long, angry gash along her side.“If that’s deep enough that something got punctured under there, you’re going to need a hospital,” Tony warned.“No-” Clint put his hand on the woman’s shoulder to stop her from getting up. “No hospitals,” she said, sinking back down and glaring around at the three of them. “No police.”“No one’s calling the police,” Clint assured her. “But you need to stay still so I can take a look at this and stitch you up.”For the most part, she followed Clint’s instructions, though she was tense the entire time. Bucky didn’t think that was due to the wound she’d come here with. From the muscles and scars all over her and the hard look in her eyes, it was obvious she was a fighter, well-used to getting hurt and getting patched up by whoever could be relied upon.No, Bucky was fairly certain this woman had expected Clint to be home alone and that her tension was due to the presence of himself and Tony as unknown quantities. Or, as unknown as they could ever be, what with Tony being Tony.“You’re keepin’ interesting company these days, Hawkeye,” she commented after he’d cleaned the wound and started stitching.“I’ve always kept interesting company,” Clint said, somewhat absently.“Sure, okay, but the Tony Stark? How the hell do you know each other?”“We’re friends,” Tony answered sharply. “And since you already know who I am, what’s your name anyway? Who are you?”“This is Javelynn,” Clint answered for the woman, which, while technically an answer, Bucky was fairly certain that hadn’t been the answer Tony had been looking for. Especially since they’d already known that from the way Clint had greeted her at the door.“Javelynn is a codename,” Tony countered, confirming Bucky’s assumption. “Tony Stark is my real name. What’s her real name?” he asked Clint directly.Clint paused his stitching, glancing between Javelynn and Tony’s faces briefly before shrugging.“I don’t know.”Tony’s eyebrows flew up his forehead.“You don’t know?” he asked incredulously.“Why would he?” Javelynn asked waspishly. “It’s not like I know his name either.”Tony stared between the two of them.“You don’t know each other’s names,” he said slowly, “but you trust him enough to show up at his apartment for medical attention? Why?”“It’s not unheard of,” Clint argued. “Daredevil and I have crashed in on each other before for help, and neither of us knows who’s behind the mask.”“You’ve been keeping tabs on the vigilantes in the city, right?” Tony asked, turning his attention to Bucky, who wanted no part of this particular back and forth but was now, unfortunately, mixed up in it anyway. “You ever heard of her before?”Bucky shook his head silently. It wasn’t out of the question that she was a lower level vigilante, or someone with a small enough patrol area that she hadn’t crossed Bucky’s radar. But he didn’t think that was the case.“Didn’t think so. So, my question stands: how do you two know each other?”Clint bit his lip and stayed quiet while he finished tying off his last stitch.“We used to be coworkers,” he said finally. There was an evasiveness to his voice that Bucky didn’t quite understand.

Chapter 1: Vienna“But you know that when the truth is told, you can get what you want or you can just get old.” - Billy Joel (Vienna 1977)Sometimes, only when he was feeling particularly hopeless, he would stare up at the ceiling of his bedroom and think of the Bukowski quote: “Are you becoming what you’ve always hated?”, and would attempt to the best of his ability to answer that. In all honesty, he had no idea. He would hate to look his ten-year-old self in the eyes now. Maybe that was telling enough? Not because he would hate who he was now, but because he would be disappointed that it wasn’t more. He had hoped for so much when he was young. Before his joints creaked and his body began to continuously protest his existence.The hope he once held became lost over time. Damn, by the time he was thirteen, it was replaced with a courage born of disparity. He hadn’t allowed himself to hope for an eternity. His twenty-year-old self would hate him, that’s for sure. Finishing up Seminary School, feeling like he found his place in the world, among the people. A life of modest means and immeasurable understanding of the world. He was more than ready to take the oath of the priesthood and finally feel wanted by something. His thirty-year-old self wouldn’t hate him; he would just be disappointed that he was no longer the diplomat of peace he once preened himself to be, begging to be called. That he was now an ancient, washed-out bureaucrat who could no longer believe in the good of people.“That’s who you are now, Thomas,” he whispered to himself in the quiet darkness. “A lonely old bureaucrat.”He rolled over on his side, much to his body's protest, and reached for his phone, charging on his bedside table. The bright white light of the phone blinded him momentarily as he checked the time: 2:45 am. He had been lying in bed spiraling for over two hours. At this point, he should just accept the fact that sleep once again had evaded him.The feeling of restlessness was normal to him now, but not quite in the traditional sense of the word. He didn’t feel like he was running from rest but rather attempting to chase it down himself. He felt tired, in all truth. For lack of a better word, he felt like shit.He was no stranger to the feeling of ‘shit’. He could describe the past year as one perpetual cycle of feeling like shit. It wasn’t his fault, in all honesty. He got his diagnosis six months ago, and in that moment, he was ready to refuse treatment and let God take him, pleading it was his time. The doctor looked at him with kind eyes and told him there was a support group for men diagnosed with cancer. He shook his head slowly with his jaw clenched tight.“Do you at least have someone to talk to about this? Cancer is exhausting both physically and mentally.” The doctor asked Thomas, who was trying his hardest not to burst out into tears. Be strong, Thomas, you have to be strong, repeated in his mind as he blinked back tears. A few escaped, sliding down his cheekbones until he tasted the salt on his lips.“I have friends I can talk to…” Thomas offered with a weak smile. The doctor nodded, writing down a note on paper in front of him.“You live alone, yes?” Thomas internally rolled his eyes at the question. Thanks for reminding me, he thought as he eyed the doctor’s wedding band with a twinge of jealousy.“That’s correct, yes.” He responded.“We could send someone to check up on you every few days if yo-“ Thomas cut the man off quickly. “That won’t be necessary.” The doctor raised an eyebrow in response and continued. “Mr. Lawrence, I understand the situation you are in as well as the pain that is to come- please, not just for my sake, or your friends, reach out to a psychologist.” He pushed a paper across the desk with a name and phone number Thomas didn’t even bother to read.On his drive back from the hospital, he took a slight detour. Instead of discussing the diagnosis with anyone, not even his sister Evita or his closest friend Aldo, he stopped by a liquor store to buy the most expensive bottle of wine he could find. Four hundred dollars. Thomas scoffed at the outrageous price but proceeded to tap his credit card on the reader without a blink. Brown paper bag in hand, he made his way to the car, feeling numb inside even without the alcohol.Thomas had not drank for the purpose of getting drunk in many years, mostly because he hated the feeling of not being in control. Yet being in control of his life right now seemed not to be going too great for him. He drove back to his apartment in silence- no radio, no podcast, not even the windows rolled down. He felt numb, but knew with some help he could somehow feel even less.He forgoed grabbing a wine glass, opting to drink straight from the bottle. He sat on his small balcony overlooking Washington, D.C. Honestly, it really could not even be considered a balcony as it was only large enough to fit a small chair he used for reading and a small table he chose to set the wine bottle on.

The craft services table was the worst. No, scratch that—it was the absolute worst. Tiny, overcrowded, and smelling faintly of burnt coffee, it stretched out awkwardly along the back of the soundstage, half of it stacked with sad pastries and the other half with a sadder assortment of fruit that had clearly seen better days.
Eric Winter ducked under a low-hanging light fixture, holding his mug like it was a lifeline. He had volunteered to grab the first round, but Melissa O’Neil had bounded in beside him before he could even think about reaching the coffee urn.
“Nope,” she said firmly, looping her arm through his. “We’re in this together.”
Eric gave her a pointed look. “You do realize this is basically a line from hell, right?”
Melissa grinned. “All the better for bonding.”
It started innocently enough. A few extras shuffled past, muttering about who got there first, who was allowed the last banana, who had dared to touch the last muffin. Within five minutes, however, it had descended into utter chaos. One extra—whose nametag Eric never even caught—was sneezing like a machine gun, each blast more dramatic than the last, while another was loudly recounting their entire life story to anyone within earshot. A toddler extra wandered into the fray, chased by a frazzled PA, and somehow Eric and Melissa ended up acting as an impromptu blockade.
Melissa poked at a muffin with a tentative finger. “Are these… alive?”
Eric snorted, trying to dodge the sneeze-fest. “Pretty sure one of them just growled at me.”
By now, both of them had given up on looking dignified. Melissa started a running commentary. “Watch this,” she whispered, elbowing Eric. “He’s about to spill it. I can feel it in my soul.”
Eric raised an eyebrow, smirking. “And I’m supposed to be professional,” he muttered, though he was clearly entertained. “We have officially reached peak craft services chaos.”
Somewhere between dodging a flying croissant and a man trying to juggle three coffee cups at once, they discovered a mutual talent: roasting the extras with subtle, sarcastic commentary that was just quiet enough to be safe. Melissa mimed the sneezy guy turning into a soap opera villain; Eric added a flourish, pretending the woman narrating her life story was plotting a coup to take over all of craft services.
The pair ducked behind a giant cooler for cover as a rogue toddler extra made a run for the muffins. Eric leaned over, whispering, “We’re basically heroes right now. The unsung heroes of breakfast.”
Melissa snorted. “And someday they’ll write songs about us. Or at least a small, niche Twitter thread.”
By the time they finally reached the front of the line, they were practically glowing with mischief. Coffee cups in hand, they stared at the muffins as if daring them to fight back.
Melissa squinted at Eric. “You know what we need?”
Eric raised an eyebrow. “Enlighten me.”
“A secret handshake.” Melissa gestured dramatically at the muffins. “Something no one else can know. Something forged in the fires of craft services chaos.”
Eric’s smirk turned into a grin. “I’m intrigued. Hit me.”
And so, they invented it. It began with a series of clumsy high-fives, progressed to a shoulder bump, included a dramatic finger snap, and ended with them balancing the muffin precariously on their heads as a final flourish. They added a secret grunt, a synchronized lean, and a pretend nod of mutual respect. It was completely ridiculous—and completely perfect.
The PA’s nearby gave them a strange look. Melissa waved cheerfully. “Don’t mind us! Just… bonding over muffins!”
By the time they returned to set, coffee in hand, muffins mostly intact, and faces flushed with laughter, they both knew that something had shifted. Craft services could be chaotic, absurd, and borderline dangerous, but in that tiny line, they had found something rare: a moment of pure, shared silliness.
“Next time,” Eric said, taking a sip of his lukewarm coffee, “we bring a stopwatch and make this a full-scale event. Official craft services Olympics.”
Melissa laughed so hard she almost dropped her muffin. “Deal. But I get the gold medal for ‘Best Dodger of Rogue Toddler Extra.’”
Eric grinned. “Fine, but I call the secret handshake title. No one else can know about it.”
“Agreed,” Melissa said, grinning back. “Forever ours.”
And for the rest of the day, every glance they exchanged—between takes, during blocking, even over walkie-talkies—was laced with the memory of that chaotic little moment. The craft services line had been awful. The muffins were terrible. But somehow, in the chaos, they’d made a memory that was theirs alone.

There was a lot that could be said about the issues that came with children and how those issues impacted Slade and Alex once their son was born, but even Alex had to admit the worst of it had to be the lack of sleep. Slade had his own issues when it came to sleep, and once Conner was born, he refused to let the infant sleep without him there next to him. Alex sometimes wondered if this was more for Slade's benefit than it was for Conner's benefit, but he wasn't about to start that conversation. Alex was the one that had taken on most of the night time care that came with Conner, as he was a workaholic who was able to function on a limited amount of sleep, but to the misfortune of them both, that seemed to be an inherited trait. Conner kept them both awake as much as he could, and on the occasions the child did sleep, it was when neither Alex nor Slade could. It was almost torturous, and after several months of this and more than a few examinations done, Alex instilled a strict routine that would ensure the two of them could at least receive a few hours of sleep. It worked, or at least it worked until it didn't. Alex swore sometimes that Conner inherited more from Slade than he did from him, even with no DNA involvement.“He should have been in bed three hours ago.” Alex noted as he rested on the couch, unable to miss how the infant held onto the other man like he was his comfort item. “This is the kind of shit he inherits from you.”“He loves me.” Slade reasoned as he moved a blanket to cover both him and the child, not missing the irritated look that was thrown at him in return. “He inherits that from you.”“I'm tired.” Alex muttered as he tried to take what rest he could receive without sleep, hesitating for a moment before he continued. “What's your excuse for the breastfeeding attempts?”“He never does that to me.” Slade reasoned in a matter-of-fact kind of manner, unable to miss the irritated look the other man continued to hold over this fact. “You are the mother—”“Oh, fuck you.” Alex spat out as he made his offense over the statement clear, crawling off the couch before he headed towards the bedroom. “You can take the first shift because of that statement.”“Alex, don't be like that.” Slade called out in a hushed kind of tone, taking notice of the little yawn their son expressed before he spoke again. “I'll be there in a bit.”There was no denial about the fact that parenthood could be hard, but this was a fact that Alex and Slade were forced to learn firsthand in recent months. Alex nor Slade would ever trade that hell for anything in the world, though, as they knew how hard the loss of a child could be. It had occurred to them both far too many times for comfort. Conner was theirs, and he would be taken care of no matter what.

The smell of scorched earth was supposed to bother you. Most people disliked the smell, that bitter tang of ash that meant a habitat had been reduced to nothing. But to you, it smelled like potential. You crouched among the blackened soil of the Crimson Lions’ training field, brushing away the fine layer of soot with the back of your glove. Underneath, the first stubborn sprouts of green were already pushing through.“Life doesn’t waste time,” you murmured to yourself, jotting notes in your worn journal.“Nor should it,” a calm voice replied from behind you. You looked up, startled and standing there was  Fuegoleon Vermillion, tall and unshakably composed. The red cloak of his squad draped over his shoulders like a flame frozen mid-movement. His gaze was sharp but not unkind, violet eyes taking in both you and the field as though he were cataloging details for later reflection.“Captain Vermillion,” you greeted, standing and brushing ash from your knees. “Apologies if I’m intruding on your squad’s training grounds.”“Not at all,” he said, approaching with measured steps. “Captain Yami informed me one of his members would be conducting ecological research here. I confess I was… curious.”That made you smile. “About the research?”“About why anyone would wish to study a wasteland.”You laughed softly. “That’s the thing about fire, Captain. It destroys, yes, but it also makes room for something new. I want to understand how that happens. How magic can hurt and heal at the same time.”For a moment, his expression softened. He knelt beside you, gloved hand hovering over a patch of soil. A faint shimmer of flame flickered in his palm not enough to burn, just enough to warm the air. “The Salamander’s flames bring both destruction and rebirth,” he said quietly. “Even the fiercest fire obeys the will of its master.”You tilted your head, curious. “And do you ever wish you could turn it off? The fire, I mean.”He looked at you then really looked, and you felt the weight of that gaze. “Fire is what I am. But I am learning… that not all warmth requires burning.”Something about that stayed with you.Over the next few weeks, your visits became routine. You’d collect samples and take notes while the Crimson Lions trained nearby, their roars and explosions forming a strange kind of background music. Fuegoleon would appear at intervals, often with a simple, “You are unharmed, I trust?” or “Have you made progress?”Each time, you’d tell him about the new shoots emerging in the ash, the resilient plants adapting to scorched soil. Each time, he’d listen, not out of obligation, but genuine interest.One afternoon, as the sun dipped low, you found him waiting for you at the edge of the field.“I had my squad clear this section for you,” he said, gesturing to a newly tilled patch of soil. “I thought it might aid your research.”You blinked, touched. “You didn’t have to do that.”“I wanted to,” he said simply. “You see things others overlook. That deserves encouragement.”You smiled, heart tightening in your chest. “That’s very kind, Captain.”He hesitated, a rare thing for him, then said, “Fuegoleon. When we are not addressing our squads, you may call me Fuegoleon.”The warmth in your cheeks had nothing to do with his magic. “Then you should call me (Y/N)."He inclined his head slightly, a ghost of a smile touching his lips. “(Y/N), then.” Silence fell, not awkward but charged with something unspoken, something that flickered between you like the faint glow of embers.You looked down at the soil, at the green that persisted through fire. “It’s funny,” you said softly. “I used to think your element and mine were opposites. But maybe they’re not so different. Fire burns, plants grow, both need each other to keep the world alive.”Fuegoleon watched you for a long moment before replying. “Perhaps that is why we keep meeting here, where flame and life cross paths.” His tone was calm, but there was something in his eyes that made your breath catch, a quiet admiration, deep and steady, like the heart of a flame that never goes out.And as the sun set behind him, casting his hair in molten gold and his cloak in crimson light, you realized something simple but profound: He wasn’t just the embodiment of fire. He was warmth made human. And somehow, you had found yourself growing toward him, like a sprout reaching for the heat that gives it life.
