He remembered the touch of her skin, soft and warm and giving, dimpling, deforming under his fingers. He remembered the smell of her hair, light and floral like sunlight falling through the dappled leaves, at the same time smoky with the sparks of a wood fire. He remembered the sound of her laugh, bold and fearless, an invitation and a declaration, a challenge, as enticing as an apple to a wanderer dying of thirst after a series of bad decisions.She was the bad decision. He was not a wanderer, still isn’t, but he was and still is a man dying of thirst, throat parched as dry as the desert in the west, the fires of desire scorching him from the inside out, devouring him in bloodlust and battle-hunger, the flames fanning out and ravaging everything he’s ever touched.She might have been a bad decision, but he fell into it willingly, dropped to his knees in front of her butterfly-embroidered coat and kissed it reverently, buried his face in the warm wool and breathed a prayer, hoping for it to be answered.And answer she did, with a hand on his head, the heat bypassing his hair and burning his scalp, the small hand with the elegant fingers and bulky rings, night-painted nails barely scraping the roots of his sunset hair. She said his name, and he lifted his head, gazing at the glint in her eyes like allegiance, like faith, like devotion.And said, Let me be the one.
And am I supposed to run away from home?
The city was long gone, crumbling ruins in a desolate land, rotting wood and weathered stone littering the patchy grass like abandoned shrines. But he recognized the buildings nonetheless—or what they once were. The restaurant, the grocer, the wine-maker, the toy-seller. And in the midst of it all, a rusted green doll, still and silent like the hunk of metal it pretended it never was. Upon approach, it clanked, metal screeching across metal with a shower of sparks, then shuddered, a pathetic attempt to draw itself upright, and groaned, Ad astra abysso—abyssoq—Ad astra—Ad astra—Ad—Ad—Ad—A blade of water plunged into the cavity of its chest, gleaming in the golden light of the afternoon sun, shattering the delicate mechanisms of the artificial voice box. The doll fell silent, the last sounds of its programmed dialogue lingering in the silence like a paean, echoing off the mountains to their right: Ad astra abyssoque, ad astra, ad astra.A blessing, once.He turned away. He didn’t need those blessings of old, not anymore, not for a long time coming. Once, it had been a blessing to sit and watch the passage of time, the leaves of the tree outside his window changing from gold to crimson to emerald and to gold again, cycle after cycle, year after year. He watched the daughter of the innkeeper toddle towards the street, then walk into it holding her mother’s hand, skip down it with her school friends, run towards the young man waiting at the other end, stroll along it with her husband, and finally toddle once again, against the physician’s advice.He had watched as the sun rose and set over the ocean, its waves sparkling and glinting, sending those sharp spikes of light into his eyes, piercing at the tears he hadn’t even known he’d shed. And through it all, through all these years, he’d heard her voice, the whisper of a ghost on the wind, berating him for his weakness, tempting him with possibilities, but most of all teasing him, laughing at him for the choice he’d made, the so-called blessing that was his reward from his god.You don’t stand a chance, she crooned by his ear, an imitation of the girl he’d once held. You’ll regret it one day, you’ll see.He waved the specter away, dismissing its pointless drivel. This thing, whatever it was, didn’t understand him at all. That was how he knew it wasn’t real, wasn’t actually her. She knew, had told him upon first setting eyes upon him, that they were one and the same, hearts burning with foolishness, unrepentantly and doggedly trudging the path they chose. She knew, better than anyone, that he had no regret, not for a single thing he’d done, because neither did she.But maybe…His gaze turned to a glint of gold beside his feet, a flash of brightness—the sun’s last gift of the day before sinking below the horizon, that wine-dark sea. He bent, brushed the dirt away, picked up the butterfly hair clip. It wasn’t hers, of course not, but his first thought was that it must have been. Who else, after all? Who else would?The pall of night fell upon his shoulders, tinting his world navy blue. He sat, turned the clip in his hands, its sharp edges cutting painfully, satisfyingly, into his skin, and thought that maybe he already regretted it.

Title: Welcome to the Land of Capitallism (Feat. the_absurdist_spectrum)
[All power has a price.]
[You have received a Flaw.]
[Your Flaw is:…]
Sunny read the runes, and his eyes widened with horror. The glee he had for receiving his aspect retreated deep into his mind, buried under layers among layers of worry.
‘Oh, no. No, no, no…’
He closed his eyes, then opened them again, hoping that this was just a dream, or a revelation.
But his flaw had already taken effect. With a single whisper, the spell had taken everything from him.
The runes were still there, shining brightly, as though mocking him.
Flaw: [Clear conscience].
Flaw description: [You cannot lie.]
Sunny stared at those three simple words, feeling like there was a bottomless abyss opening right beneath his feet. The Spell was usually frivolous with its descriptions, but it decided to be straight and on the point this time — there were only 3 words.
‘Can’t lie. I can’t lie? Me? How am I supposed to live if I can’t lie?!’
Lifting his head, he stared into the deep void, the shimmering runes in front of him shining brightly, as if mocking his fate.
He gritted his teeth, before letting it all out.
“I demand a do over!” He screamed, “What Awakened Tyrant shows up at a First Nightmare?! I almost died, you damned Spell! And now you give me this flaw?”
“I swear I’ll find whoever’s behind you and kill them!” He spat, and yet, nothing changed.
“Well… what have I been expecting anyways? There’s no way the Spell would respond…’
Shaking his head, Sunny began to read the description again, desperately praying that he was wrong. But at the moment, a new set of runes appeared in front of him, the Spell’s indifferent voice resounding in the black void.
[You have sworn at the Spell.]
[A special achievement has been unlocked!]
[You have received an -unknown- blessing.]
[Child of Shadows, receive your boon!]
Under Sunny’s astonished eyes, the ridiculous runes continued.
‘What… What is this?’
[You have received the permission to access the Customer Service Line.]
[Access currently opened.]
[the_absurdist_spectrum has joined the chat.]
[the_absurdist_spectrum: No.]
[the_absurdist_spectrum has left the chat.]
Sunny stared at the words, he had never heard of the Spell having a Customer Service Line! This… this couldn’t be real, could it?
“...Is this a dream?” He muttered, bewildered.
[the_absurdist_spectrum has joined the chat.]
[the_absurdist_spectrum: Nope. And don't bother me. I'm trying to pet a flying cockroach right now. Call me when you get to that damned tree. Adios.]
[the_absurdist_spectrum has left the chat.]
Staring blankly, only one question slipped out of Sunny's mind.
"...what the hell is an Adios?"
[Thank you for using our Customer Service Line!]
‘No–’
Just as Sunny was about to curse at the attitude of the Spell, another set of runes appeared.
[Wake up, Lost from Light!]
The black void spun and disappeared.
Sunny opened his eyes.
—
After some time…
[You have acquired a drop of ichor. Do you wish to consume it?]
Sunny blinked.
Consume… a Memory?
Things were getting weirder and weirder. Just like that Customer Service Line at the end of his First Nightmare… That was the last time he saw it — no matter how much he desired for it to appear, nothing would happen. Like that scene from last time was but a dream.
But it couldn’t be wrong! His eyes were right, he knew what he saw.
Unless… he had to get to the ‘damned tree’, or whatever the Spell meant by that.
‘Damnation! Isn’t this already hard enough!? How am I supposed to know which tree it is?!’
…
He might as well try taking the ichor. Nothing would happen, right?
“Yes. I want to consume it.”
[As you wish.]
The golden sphere separated into two streams of beautiful, radiant liquid. It flowed through the air, approaching his face with alarming speed. Briefly, it gently touched his cheeks, before changing its direction, and moved up, head towards…
‘My eyes?!’
When Sunny realized this, it was already too late to do anything — the golden liquid had already reached the point, even flowing into his eyes, entering his soul through his pupils.
Soon, it was gone.
Sunny froze, not knowing what to expect.
A second passed, then another.
Raising his trembling hands to his face, Sunny’s mouth twisted into a desperate grin — he felt something. Finally.
In the next moment, Sunny opened his mouth, and let out a terrible, wailing shriek as unimaginable, blinding pain tore through his entire being.
As he screamed, his whole body convulsed in spasms of terrible pain, his mind drowning in the endless torrent of excruciating suffering.
He clawed as his face, leaving bloody marks on it, desperate for some kind of distraction from the sheer torture he signed himself with. And yet, a few seconds later, they were gone — erased by some unknown force.
He flinched in disbelief, staring at his own two hands, and…
Oh. His voice was gone as well.
But the pain continued.
Powerless to stop it, Sunny had no choice, but to endure it.
Tick tock.
Tick

The usual cacophony weaved around Darth Vader as he stood at the centre of the Executor’s bridge. Captains, lieutenants and officers of every military ranking moved around him like waves, their voices hushed and businesslike. Fingertips tapped out commands on keyboard consoles, footsteps echoed on the permacrete floor, and droids beeped as they scuttled back and forth between the main docking bay, control rooms, and navigation centre.
The crown jewel of imperial engineering, the Executor carved through hyperspace as it always did, meticulous in its design and precise in its calculation. The personnel aboard his flagship were paragons of discipline, unmatched throughout the empire in skill and efficiency. Additionally, his own plans were proceeding according to schedule. Luke remained in their private training facility, exactly where Vader had left him earlier that day. For the first time in two decades, Vader’s life felt stable and dare he say…peaceful.
And yet.
A disturbance in the Force lingered at the fringes of his awareness, like a faint, nagging whisper that Vader found impossible to disregard. He concentrated, poked at the cloud of unease, tried to crack it open and bend it to his will, but…nothing. The sensation was maddeningly elusive and difficult to discern, and Vader’s frustration mounted.
Something was wrong. But what?
His thoughts drifted to his son, and he tugged on the Force bond linking them. Luke usually responded to the action swiftly, but this time, he took a second too long to answer. Vader frowned at the unexpected delay.
Are you well? he asked.
Yeah, I’m fine, came Luke’s reply. He sounded distant and unfocused, as though he had travelled light-years away.
Vader shifted slightly and glanced upwards, as if he could peer through layers of durasteel, circuitry, and machinery into Luke’s quarters.
Son?
No answer.
Vader tensed. It was unlike his son to act so distracted and disengaged. It had been Luke who initiated contact after the disaster of Bespin, Luke who chose to live aboard the Executor, Luke who had bridged the chasm between them and brought a semblance of normalcy into Vader’s existence. Annabeth couldn't believe that she had found the statue - it felt like she would wake up and realize that this was, in fact, not happening. But it was real, she had done what none had done before her, and found the Parthenos.
She had become not just a child of Athena, but the child of Athena - the one who restored her mother’s legacy.

Ha! Serves her right.
Annabeth barely had a moment to process the grandeur of the statue before the room shook - her heart plummeted, realizing that she may not have been victorious at all. What if the room just collapsed, killing her and destroying the Parthenos? Considering how easily other portions of the cavern caved in, it wasn't at all outside the realm of possibilities.
Bracing herself to feel the ceiling fall on her, Annabeth crouched down and covered her head, discarding her makeshift crutch, wincing in advance. Light spilled into the cavern, and she was elated to hear the voice of Piper calling down to her, “Annabeth! Are you okay?”
Annabeth looked up, coughing a few times as the dust settled around the rubble. Luckily, the statue seemed unharmed. “Yeah, I’m alright!” Annabeth called back up as the Argo II lowered its rope ladder. As Piper began to descend, Annabeth yelled, “I think my ankle is sprained, though!”
As the others came down the rope ladder (including Nico - Annabeth was happy to see him safe), Piper slotted herself under Annabeth's arm and supported her as they made their way toward the giant version of Annabeth's mother.

Annabeth opened her mouth to answer, but Nausithoe beat her to it. “Sort of. Gods can change their size however they want. Remember when my father came onto the ship, before we crossed into the ancient lands? He usually appears much taller, because both of my uncles always present at least as tall as Ephialtes. None of them like to be shorter than any of the others.”
Annabeth rolled her eyes. Know-it-all.
“That doesn’t matter. Can we get my giant mom onboard?”

The sons of Mars and Jupiter hopped off the ladder, bearing several cables and ropes - hopefully enough to secure the Parthenos, at least. “At the very least we can secure it on the deck,” Piper added, adjusting Annabeth as she winced, “or in the stables, I guess. We’ll probably need to get it out soon either way.”
Frank walked toward the statue, but something caught his eye. “What is that?” he asked, gesturing toward the pit.
As if realizing that no one had acknowledged it, the pit seemed to give off an even more foul stench than before.
Grimly, Annabeth replied, “Tartarus.”
An audible pause rippled through the cavern, a few gazes uncomfortably flickering toward Nico. “Please be careful.” Jason advised, voicing everyone's thoughts.
Annabeth couldn't agree more. Once Frank, Leo, Jason, and Hazel began to secure the statue, she realized how strong Arachne's webs were. Jason tripped over a few, nearly falling flat on his face, before Annabeth shared what she knew.
“Be careful of the webs. I'm not sure what they’re made of, but they're not ordinary spiderwebs. Arachne said that the webs hold this room together, we don’t want to disturb more than we have to.”
“Good point.” Piper agreed, inspecting Annabeth until something caught her eye. “Nytha?”
The woman hummed in recognition from where she was sitting with her cousin. Nico was staring at Tartarus as if the pit had done him a personal wrong - and in a way, it had, Annabeth supposed.
“There’s a few threads on Annie's feet, can you get them off? I don't want her to trip when she's already hurt.”
The seventeen year old gestured at her senior's feet - in particular her sprained ankle. Annabeth wasn't quite sure how she had missed the amount of webs that had built up, but it wasn't the most pressing issue, so she brushed it off.
Nausithoe made her way over and gently cut off the threads from Annabeth's injury, wiping the sticky residue on her bare legs - Annabeth was impressed by how much they could mostly ignore each other now. It was a milestone that she would’ve thought impossible when she was twelve.
Nausithoe quickly turned back to her pseudo-brother, wrapping her arm around him as they quietly spoke.
Leo was beginning to climb up the ladder to lift the secured statue onboard when Nico yelped.
He was scrambling to his feet while the daughter of Poseidon was being dragged across the room, over rubble. Her left leg led the way, getting almost as scraped up as her hands as she frantically grabbed anything she could.

Sometimes Simon had dreams, like flashbacks of when he was in coma after an accident. The thoughts he had, the feeling of someone calling for him and trying to reach him constantly but he never being capable of reaching them, the fear of chasing them and then being met by a complete void.
And it all repeated again and again. Or he would have memories of the best moments he had with Wilhelm. The time they first went on a date at an ice-cream parlor, their first time, their first touch, first kiss.
It was all so sensitive to remember. He felt tears kissing his cheeks as his eyes slowly opened again. The first thing he saw was the ceiling and the light from the post from the street that was going through the curtain. And then, in the almost dark, Wilhelm, looking at him while supporting himself on his elbow.
A soft and slow voice came from his mouth — Simon, are you okay? You were sobbing…
And then he remembered why he had tears on his skin. The sadness came back and the want to cry was strong, making his eyes teary and his lips shaking. — I remembered… — he exhaled, trying to push the tears back and swallowed dry, putting his shaky voice on the back of his throat as he tried to speak again. — …of when I was in the hospital. The flashbacks I had nonstop. It was terrifying, Wille.
As he finished saying, the tears immediately came back and now were once again going down his face.
A hand came to rest on his face after it wiped out the tears with his thumb. Now the same thumb was brushing the cheek.
— I know, I know. I’m here, okay? It’s okay, I’m not going anywhere. You’re not going anywhere.
The sweet words were too much. He knew it was to comfort him, and it did, but it also meant that he was someone’s person, Wilhelm’s person. He cared about him and was with him in the happiest moments and the most hurtful ones. He stayed, he took care of him. And just that made him emotional, so much the tears didn’t stop coming.
The sheets made sounds, indicating that Wilhelm was coming closer, wrapping his arms around Simon, hands massaging his back while Simon’s fingers tightened in his shirt.
After all, Wilhelm came back to him. No, he stayed. The three days his eyes didn’t open, he was still there. And he was still there now, arms ready to reach for him whenever he wanted. And it did reach him.
He shouldn’t be scared anymore. Those tears were happy ones now that he has entirely wrapped around this thought.
— I love you. Thank you. — he said quietly, the constant crying messing with his voice.
— I love you, too. — the words came out in a whisper.
They waited until Simon stopped crying and calmed his breathing, consequently making his hiccups stop. Wilhelm’s comforting words and kisses worked as always. He made sure Simon was okay after he heard the little exhale he gave, which he knew perfectly that it meant the curly was tired.
He kissed him a last time on his forehead before lying down again, now with Simon squeezed against his chest, both with their hands around each other, intertwined like one, and finally going back to sleep.

Once upon a time, two husbands were engaged in a cave through a poppy. They then stumbled upon a flower valley to call home, the same way they’d stumbled into their marriage: a sweet chain of happy accidents. All this they did before their world became bloodstained.
The blue border rose on two sides of their valley, and so did the stone and dirt hills around. It felt like a bird’s nest. Flowers were dotted everywhere, a barrage of pink, purple, orange, red, yellow, blue, the husbands named it and the flowers were there. The peaceable face of the lake wrinkled when it smiled, rippling the cotton clouds into ribbons, sending the sunlight darting like schools of fish. Scott had chanced upon the idea of building holes into the wall, further bringing home the impression of a nook in a corner of nowhere. A hole in a hole in the biggest hole of all, this storm cloud of a death game blowing over. It hadn’t quite reached them yet.
It felt like nothing could touch them here. The husbands thrived. They grew sugarcane to harvest when it was tall enough; they planted seeds to reap wheat when it grew; and they made hidey-holes, hobbit homes, for when they returned home. They languished, blissfully drifting in a sea of time. So what if outside, others died to creepers, fell into traps, couldn’t spare a moment not looking over their shoulder? For laughable fear. The husbands built a wall around their enclosed valley and textured it as a reminder that there was time for beauty.
Scott had a plan for how their home would look. “When this is all over,” he said, “I’ll shear some leaves and spruce up the place with fake bushes. Maybe I’ll add a waterfall or two.”
He would smile. The light would dance off his cheeks.
“That would be cute. Like, right there, or there…”
Jimmy never talked about the inclement weather, the storm clouds on the breeze. Instead he would reply, “Yeah, that would be nice,” and he would think about what home looked like when all the carnage was over.
They had forgotten while remembering that they were not excluded from the killing, the thirst for blood, or more than that, survival. They had assumed without believing that they would be alive at the end.
It was home. The place had a magnetic effect. A mysterious quality.
As it had to, the world fell apart and broke into three factions. The husbands could hide no longer. They had to take a stand. For the last time, which they did not know, or else they would have stood rooted to the ground and died as trees on the land of their home, they scrounged for potions and left the flower valley, with its walls, its two homes, and the poppies blooming in the grasses.
They ran to the desert, where their allies hatched a plan, a last resort. A biome rigged with TNT, designed to take out all their enemies in one fell swoop.
Scott was on green, but he had qualms about the explosives beneath the flimsy sand, the infinite possibilities for things to backfire. Along the line, his careless, easily shocked, overly curious husband had fallen to his last life. Skin grey and eyes red, he looked nothing like the hero he had been when he was healthy, happy and content, but it was still him. It was him after all.
Jimmy stood in the bunker, pacing back and forth, his eyes peeking out. The cerulean sky held not a sliver of cloud, but a storm began to brew in the husbands’ heart.
It would be fine. And even if it would not, what else could they do? Watch like sitting ducks before the enemy came for their home?
“They’re coming! They’re running in!”In the bunker, Jimmy could do nothing, trapped by a layer of obsidian and sandstone. That lever would cause disaster, and he wouldn’t have to use that button, hopefully. The rain was unexpected, according to the rest of N25. This kind of downpour was, at least.
Ena had insisted that it would be a gentle sprinkle at worst. And it was, at first, something she'd gotten cocky about.
“Told you so,” Ena had teased. “Look how light this is.”
It was Mizuki’s turn to laugh, though, when that sprinkle eventually became a drumming downpour that turned the pavement into a mirror, their outing into a game of ducking from awning to awning, and selfie-ready Ena into a sopping, grumbling mess.
“Hmm. Hey, guys—” Mizuki put on her best shit-eating grin as she reached into her bag— “guess who brought an umbrella?”
“You did,” Mafuyu sighed, glancing up. A bit of water dropped directly onto her nose, and she wiped her face with her sleeve.
Kanade giggled. She didn’t seem to mind the weather. Something about the rain feeling like home, she’d said once. They kept walking, puddles forming around their feet.
Mizuki fell behind, stepping out from under their shelter, and opened the umbrella with a flourish and a fwoosh.
Ena rolled her eyes and shook a bit of wetness out of her hair. “Ah, shut up. Not all of us are gonna be prepared for a tropical storm.”
Mizuki twirled her umbrella, sending a fine spray of water onto Ena’s shirt. “Honestly, guys,” she said, voice bright even over the tapping of the rain. “As much as you’re on the internet, you’d think you guys would check a weather app once in a while.”
The rain only got louder as they went, building to a steady roar against umbrellas and awnings, blurring the world into watercolor. Mizuki twirled her umbrella again, gently, watching the droplets spin off its edges in a spiral and vanish into the river forming along the curb.
The rest of the group ducked under yet another storefront overhang, shaking themselves off like wet cats. Mizuki stepped a little ahead, peering over the glare of streetlights smearing across the pavement. She didn’t get out all that much outside of school anymore. When she did, she saw the little parts of the world with a glimmer of wonder in her eyes.
The rest of N25’s voices blurred under the rain’s rhythm, a backdrop she wandered out of without meaning to.
She saw, in the corner of her eye, through the shifting veil of raindrops, a shape slouched on a bench in a grassy area. No umbrella, no motion. It blurred at the edges, like it was letting the rain wash it away.
The rain shifted, then, and wind tilted her umbrella.
A flash of color, too bright and too stubborn to be washed out by the storm. Violet. A splash of blue.
That fuckass outfit.
Her breath hitched, just a little.
She’d recognize Kamishiro Rui anywhere.
Mizuki rolled her eyes. She couldn’t help but smile, though.
Walking his way was almost automatic. No moment of hesitation before she shifted her path to meet him. Her body moved before her mind could ask it why.
“I’ll be back,” she called to Kanade, Ena, and Mafuyu. “Don’t wait. I’ll catch up.”
She didn’t wait for their responses—she’d started toward Rui before she thought to tell them. She let the rain swallow the chatter behind her, breaking into a half-run. The grass flecked water at her legs with every step. Chilly, but she didn’t mind it much.
The world felt quieter, the air colder the closer she got to him. He was silent, slouched over, looking defeated in a way she hadn’t seen him since…
…Hm.
Her footsteps softened on the soaked grass beside him.
“Hey, Rui,” she sing-songed, tilting her umbrella.
Rui didn’t look up.
“Mizuki,” he said, flatly.
Something in her chest pinched.
Right. So that’s the kind of day it was.
She sighed softly. “Here,” she said, ducking closer and holding the umbrella between them—an offer.
Rui’s eyes seemed to sparkle when she looked into them like this.
Without a word, he looked away and pushed her hand back—gentle, careful, almost apologetic.
“Oh my god. Fine.” The words tumbled out of Mizuki’s mouth before she knew what she was saying, but what she did next, she meant to do with every part of her:
she let go of the umbrella. It fell, hitting the grass with a small thud. And then they were equally rain-soaked.
Rui blinked. There were little drops of rain clinging to his lashes, and it made something in her flutter.
“Scoot,” Mizuki said. “You’re hogging the bench with that sad aura.”
He did.
She sat beside him, the wet bench cold under her. Not too close, but close enough that she knew he’d talk.
“So,” she said, drawing the word out. “You look like a wet ferret, and I know you don’t do that for fun. Wanna talk about it?”
A beat.
“No.” It didn’t come out mean. Just honest. Rui always was.
“Cool. Okay. I’ll be annoying enough that you eventually will.”
Rui huffed a little laugh and gave a grin he only ever seemed to with her.
“Hehe, there it is,” Mizuki teased. “I knew you could still smile.”
She playfully shoved Rui, and she watched him loosen up a bit. He giggled again, small and genuine.

One floor onto another, until there are no more floors. She thinks she hears Boden say her name or tell her to stop.But she’s already running.Back into the building, into the smoke that covers her eyes like a blanket. There is no more roof over her head. Friends showed they were thinking of each other.It was, as they say, the thought that counts.And for four years, for one thousand, four hundred and sixty-one days, that was all it was. A thought. A stubborn, persistent, one-sided gesture he refused to retract, even when he knew, for a certainty, she was throwing them away.He’d promised he would be there when she was ready. He just couldn't stay in New York to do it. The city was full of ghosts. He had betrayed her trust, and in his attempt to "protect" her, he had broken the one friendship that had fundamentally changed him.He left. He took cases. He traveled. But he left the standing order in place.The first two years were the silence. He’d heard through the grapevine (a euphemism for Fin) that the deliveries were received but not kept. He’d expected it. His intent, his justification, no longer mattered. His action was what had hurt her. The flowers weren't an apology—he knew she wouldn't accept one. They were just a presence. A quiet, floral testament: I am still here.Then, exactly two years and one week after Forlini's, his phone had lit up.The peonies are lovely. Thank you.He’d stared at the text until the words blurred. He hadn't known it was peonies. The order was simple: "Florist's choice. Fresh. No lilies." He hadn't known, until much later, that peonies were her mother’s favorite.His reply had taken an hour to compose.You’re welcome, Olivia.The silence had broken.The texts became a tentative bridge across the chasm he had created. They were sporadic. Safe.Heard you were in Madrid. Hope you're well.Saw the press conference on the cold case. Impressive, Captain.They never spoke of Wheatley. They never spoke of Stabler. They never spoke of his declaration. They spoke of cases, of the weather, of Noah. He learned her son was thriving, that he played soccer, that he missed seeing "Uncle Rafa."Each text was a careful step, a test of the fragile ground between them.Now, four years to the day, he was back.The cab from JFK was stuffy, the air thick with humidity and the smell of the city. He’d only been on U.S. soil for an hour when his phone vibrated.It wasn't a platitude about the weather.Are you in the city?His heart, that dormant, traitorous muscle, gave a painful lurch. This was it. After four years of a stubborn gesture, this was the response. This was the moment the "thought" finally became a conversation.Landed an hour ago.He watched the three dots appear and disappear. He held his breath.Drinks? Tonight? Forlini’s is gone, but I know a quiet place.The mention of the old bar was deliberate. She was acknowledging the wound. She was acknowledging the place where he had made his promise and left her. He claimed a small table in a dark corner, one that gave him a clear view of the door. This was the one jury he'd never been able to sway, the one verdict that mattered. He’d spent four years waiting, and now he felt utterly, terrifyingly unprepared. She was just Liv tonight.Their eyes met. The noise of the bar faded to a dull hum. He stood, a reflexive gesture of courtesy.She crossed the room, her expression unreadable. She stopped at the table. It has been 1 cycle since I started this journey, it didn’t seem to get any closer. It was a simple contract for pioneers, to survey a system that appeared out of the blue in the Hegemony’s sensors. The ripple it created in hyperspace sent shockwaves all around the core world. It was heavy, and it was rumored to be inhabited, but it’s been so long since anyone came back from it that we all believed it was some sort of monster. We brave monsters, that’s what this fleet is for.Though, there was nothing really frightening around the Persean Sector, nothing that isn’t human, I suppose. The worst we’ve had was a pirate fleet led by their leader. It’s fascinating to me how you can make a ship out of the shittiest parts you can find and still, somehow, wreck several hegemony fleets a hundred times over.What are we ought to do if this turns out to be a real, genuine monster? We fight it. We tear it down, bring it back home, and present it to the Core Worlds. The monster is gone, one so big that it sent ripples all across hyperspace, one whose mass was predicted to be equivalent to a supermassive black hole. It’s gone.According to our computers, we should be reaching that signal by the end of the month, hopefully that’s true as the crew has been really bored out here in hyperspace. I don’t blame them at all, the monotony of fixing up after storms has been terrible, and it’s not like we’re running out of any supplies since the last Hegemony outpost.All systems normalAntimatter fuel is stableExternal shield systems stableArmaments and ammunition stablePrimary engines stableWe should be fine. See you next month.
We’ve arrived.
I’ve seen hundreds of black holes in my life. That dim, black star that sought to consume all that it came across. I know how it’s surrounded by barren wastes and how captains would often speak about the monstrosities rumored to lay within. I was so used to it that I didn’t really think of those stories whenever I come across them again in my travels, so why… do I feel it now? As I stare deeply into that void, I felt a sense of calling, no—rather I felt like I was being watched, as though the black hole was the pupil of an eye, and the rocks and dust and that planet which surrounded it were the Iris.The fleet is not gonna waver. I tell them to keep an eye out for anything that might pop out. Clearly this system was more than it seems, and there might be a hostile fleet, or a hostile entity just waiting around that darkness waiting to lunge at us. What we didn’t expect, and what I alluded to earlier, was finding a planet.
It was a small, habitable planet, roughly the size of Mairaath. Although, unlike that desert wasteland, this one seemed to have more variations with its climate, a bona-fide Jewel World. I was ready to fight anything that might come to defend it, but nothing did, so I set up an expedition force to prepare a landing ship for that planet.I write this now on the planet itself. I must tell first what had occurred since we landed roughly forty-eight hours ago. When we reached the surface atmosphere, our landing ship encountered a storm of immense magnitude. It was unlike any storm we’ve seen before. Rather than being pelted by manageable hailstorms and rain, we instead got hit with rocks the size of an entire human. It scratched our hulls, our engines, it threatened to engulf our entire ship. Our only hope was having a hopefully safe crash landing and we did. Our terrible, derelict, fucked up beyond repair ship crash landed a few kilometers away from a city.If you could call it that, at least.
A massive sprawling city held up by tracks and wheels. It moves slowly, slumbering like a metal beast across the vast deserted wilderness. Black steam emerged from its numerous smokestacks, an obvious sign of industry—no, all these, all this entire city is an obvious sign of civilization whose innovation has been expanded horizontally rather than vertically. The remains of my crew approached that slumbering beast and wondered how we’re gonna get there in the first place.Of course, that question didn’t take long to answer. An hour later we were surrounded by people, humanoids. Some were taller than me, some were about my height, but all of them definitely have some form of animal features. Some are closer to their counterparts than others. They all spoke in a language that I could not parse, I was lucky enough to have bought that universal translator, but even then it took a while for it to give us any coherent sentences.We were taken in by that group, who, with the help of the translator, call themselves Columbians. They called us really unlucky to have landed here, that we weren’t the first ones to have gone here. I inquired about the other fleets and captains and they all said the same thing, that they left the system and never came back.

'And now on tonight's episode of Immortal and the Restless!'
What a bad episode. A bad show, actually. It was like a horrible car wreck Michael couldn't have looked away from for the past few decades, but honestly it was stupidly interesting. He leaned back in his green sofa, some pieces of popcorn spilled carelessly onto the floor. He'd clean it up later. This show was addicting, his eyes were glued to the screen at this rate... so much so that he practically jumped out of his seat; not when it was revealed to him for the 46th time that Clara had burnt the house down, but when the small mini door adjusted to just a specific boy's height opened suddenly.
Michael quickly snapped his gaze back to the entrance of the small room hidden in the PizzaPlex, almost worried that somebody had found the hideout. No, just Gregory of course. Moping around like he was mourning over something. In fact, Mike was almost urged to ask who died.
As the boy sat down next to him, staring at the television screen almost lifelessly, Michael let out a whole-hearted sigh.
"Alright, kid. What happened?"
Gregory took a moment. He tapped the armrest of the chair absent-mindedly, before groaning and putting his head in his hands.
"Some idiot took my neon BatDragon!!"
The man started in bewilderment for a moment, his eyes slightly squinted as if trying to make out what the hell this boy was talking about.
"Your what?"
"In a game," Gregory continued, throwing his arms up and leaning back into a chair. Oh, he was making a point.
"It's literally one of the best pets. AND it was fly ride! Some idiot named Emma sat on her lousy ass and told me she'd give something for it if I gave it first.."
"And you believed her?!"Michael exclaimed once he was done putting together the pieces. Though once he got another look at the sadness hidden behind anger on the boy's face, his own annoyance at the gullibility melted away. He sighed.
"What's her full name? She's banned from here."Mike crossed his arms. He'd make sure this girl never got to see the amazement of the Pizza-plex again, and he'd also make sure his son would get whatever neon BatDragon he was talking about back.
"I don't know her full name, it was online..."
"Then how did you know you could trust her?!"
"I DON'T KNOW!"The boy threw his arms up again, so Michael put his hands on his face. If he could remember right, Vanessa had complained about this similar scenario when she was younger. Something about being scammed for a halo. How were kids still falling for this bullshit?
"Alright.."He sat up again, removing his hands and putting one on Gregory's head, who tilted his head down in defeat.
"How about we get some ice cream, huh? We'll go to that hill you like. Then we'll get you some Freddy merch, or whatever you want."
The boy quickly looked up, his eyes practically shining like stars. Yup, always the perfect solution.
"Seriously?"
"Yeah. Get your jacket,"
Michael stood from the couch, clicking the old TV off and getting his own coat. It was cold outside at this time of year, though the breeze that rushed by him from Gregory running to grab his jacket made him warm. He hid a soft smile, glad he could at least somehow do something right for his son for once.

It’s different from what Din remembers. It should be after ten years, but still, Din is disoriented when they touch down on Ossus. There’s a landing in a huge clearing outside of the school now and a mechanics hut. A large New Republic shuttle is parked there alongside Luke’s old x-wing which looks shockingly rusted. Din hasn’t seen it in five years and feels strangely bowled over by the nostalgia that washes over him at the sight.
No one comes out to greet them as they make their way up the hill to the domed buildings that make up the Jedi Academy. Which makes sense. Every being inside that school probably felt their presence the moment they broke atmo. Din glances at Grogu and guesses that he’s already mentally greeting them, tuned into the frequency that all Force users have even if he’s abandoned his study of it. Maybe Grogu’s mind will change when he sees how far along the school has come.
Din expected a throng of students in matching robes, spinning around lightsabers, and parsing the ancient language on the paper scrolls Din had once found and delivered to Luke. But instead find them in the kitchen, casually lounged across floor cushions as they eat and listen to Luke, perched on a table across from them.
“Were you scared?” A student is asking when they come into the room.
“Yes,” Luke replies, glancing over at Din and Grogu. “But fear is the real test. And our first teacher. Isn’t that right, Grogu?”
Din is surprised when Grogu bounds across the room to hug Luke. He’s less keen on displays of affection lately, ducking away from head pats when he’s irritable. Luke and Grogu haven’t seen each other in years, but you wouldn’t know it by the way they easily embrace each other.
Maybe Grogu’s been in contact with Luke more than Din realized. Din hasn’t been open with how often he comms the Jedi either. What had been an occasional message in the old days of his consultancy for the Rangers had become a full-fledged habit. Din had felt that he and Luke had developed something like a friendship, but now, watching Luke and Grogu mentally speak to each other, he wonders if Luke had only been messaging Din to follow up on Grogu’s progress.
“Sorry to interrupt your lesson– uh, meal?”
Din isn’t sure what is happening here. Most of the students are unbothered by their entry, munching on fruit and whispering to each other. But one dark-haired, pale boy is eyeing Din with distrust. Din vaguely recognizes him as Luke’s nephew Ben, a once ten-year-old who’d happily chatted away with Grogu the last time they’d seen Luke.
“It’s a little of both,” Luke replies, sliding off the counter. He extends his hand to Din and grips him tight, blue eyes bright with a warmth that surprises Din. “And you’re both always welcome here.”
“Mandalorians? Here?” Ben remarks. His tone has the kind of petulance that Din would expect from a teenager, but there’s a darkness in his expression that makes Din frown.
Luke is unfazed. Still holding Din’s hand in his, he levels Ben with a look and says, “Grogu and his father are the reason we have the scrolls you are studying so intently these days. Now,” he says letting go of Din’s hand and turning to the rest of the students, “chores, all of you. Our guests want to speak with me.”
The students scatter without complaint, cleaning as they go. Ben shares one last lingering look with Grogu, and even underneath his helmet, Din can read the stillness of Grogu’s dislike radiate back to Ben’s sullen face.
Grogu turns sharply to follow Luke, mood palpably darker than the one he’d arrived with. But with every step across Ossus’ idyllic landscape, he seems to lighten, lifting his helmet from his head and holding his face to the sun. The same midday sunshine that glows white through the pale hair on Grogu’s head makes Luke’s into burnished gold.
There’s streaks of grey among the blonde now, Din notices, and in the short beard that adorns his chin. It makes Din unfathomably sad for some reason, the way he sometimes feels when he remembers Grogu as the young toddler that used to sleep in the crook of his arm. Time is a thief.
Luke glances at Din occasionally as they walk uphill to a large tree and pond ahead. There’s curiosity in his eyes, no doubt noting the changes in Din’s appearance. Some molecular change that he’s undergone at fifty that he hadn’t presented at forty-five.

A low wind swept across the training yard, carrying the scent of dust and steel. The morning drills had barely started when a sharp, sickening sound split through the quiet — the unmistakable thrum of mana slicing through air, followed by a dull crash.
Someone gasped. Someone else shouted for guards.
And then Kalian felt it.
A flare of killing intent — aimed at a single person.
His older brother.
Before he even registered the movement, the raven-haired prince was sprinting, boots hammering against stone. A cloud of smoke dispersed ahead, revealing a collapsed figure on the ground, blue hair scattered like spilled frost across the dirt. A thin trail of blood ran down from the blunette’s temple, dripping onto his collar.
Plants was on his knees, one hand pressed weakly against the ground. His pale blue eyes — usually cold, unwavering — were unfocused, moving as though searching for something that wasn’t there.
And his attacker, cloaked in dark cloth, stood only a few steps away, blade drawn again.
“Your Highness,” one of the mages called out, voice tight, “don’t—”
Too late.
A crimson flash burst across the courtyard.
The third prince didn’t shout. He didn’t ask anything. He simply tackled the man with the force of someone who had killed before and had no hesitation doing it again. The sound of bones cracking echoed sharply as Kalian dragged the attacker across the dirt and slammed him into a wall.
The man tried to scream.
He didn’t get the chance.
The courtyard fell into silence — until Kalian’s low voice cut through the air, cold and strangely gentle.
“You shouldn’t have touched my brother.”
By the time the healers finished, the sun had moved across half the sky. Plants sat quietly on a bench in the covered veranda, posture perfectly still, breathing steady. To anyone else, he looked composed — merely tired.
But Kalian saw the subtle tension in his jaw, the faint tremble each time a healer’s hand brushed near his face.
And most of all, he saw the eyes.
Pale blue, luminous, but unfocused. Like looking through fog. Like staring into a haze that wouldn’t clear.
“They’re not damaged,” the healer had insisted. “No physical injury remains. I’m… not sure why he still cannot see.”
Not sure.
Kalian nearly snapped the man’s neck for saying that.
Now, stepping closer, he watched as Plants slowly tilted his head, following the sound of footsteps rather than sight.
“What is it?” the blunette asked.
His voice was steady, but too quiet — the way someone spoke when the world felt unfamiliar.
The raven-haired prince sat beside him, resting an arm casually across the back of the bench as if nothing were wrong.
“You look fine,” he observed lightly.
Plants, recognizing the presence, huffed softly. “I can’t see.”
“I noticed.”
A long moment passed. The breeze carried the faint metallic scent of dried blood — not much, but enough.
The blunette inhaled once.
Then again.
“…Blood,” he murmured under his breath.
Kalian’s lips curved into a smile. “Oh? Can you still smell it? I thought quite some time had passed.”
Plants turned his head slightly, though his eyes remained unfocused. “Did you kill him?”
“No,” the younger prince said, resting his cheek on his hand, voice deceptively light. “I just took out the eyes.”
A beat.
“…I see.”
“Do you?” Kalian teased. “I thought you couldn’t.”
The older did not humor him with an answer. He simply sat still, shoulders relaxing the slightest bit — not because he approved, but because he understood. His brother acted, always, with a frighteningly direct logic.
If someone attacked the second prince, then the raven would retaliate in a way no one would forget.
“Ah—” Kalian tilted his head, studying the vacant gaze. “You’re looking the wrong way. I’m over here, brother.”
The blunette turned toward his voice, expression consistently neutral, but the faint crease between his brows betrayed his discomfort.
“Your eyes,” Kalian asked, leaning in a little, “how bad is it? Darkness? Blur?”
“Black,” Plants replied. “Everything is… black.”
“And the world is suddenly quiet, isn’t it?” Kalian murmured. “Without sight to distract you.”
The other did not answer immediately. Instead, he shifted his hand slightly toward where he assumed the younger prince sat. It brushed Kalian’s sleeve — a confirmation, silent and small.
Kalian didn’t tease him for it.
“Temporary blindness,” he said, voice softening. “The healer thinks it’ll fade.”
“And you?” Plants asked.
The raven-haired prince chuckled. “I think I’ll kill the next person who looks at you incorrectly.”
“That is not a diagnosis.”
“It’s a perfectly reasonable one.”
For a moment, the blunette fell quiet, gaze falling to his hands — hands that could fight, write, command, but could not grasp the shape of the world in front of him.
“…How long?” he asked.
“I don’t know.” Kalian leaned back, but his shoulder remained close enough to brush the other’s. “But until then, I’ll deal with things.”
A pause.
Then, quietly, “And I’ll be your eyes, if you want.”

The apartment held the winter like a breath. Heat clunked through old pipes, doing what it could against the draft sneaking under the balcony door. The city outside had dressed itself in lights it didn’t need—strings of LEDs looped around convenience store awnings, a plastic reindeer staked into the planter across the street, couples moving in twos with paper bags and fogged-up glasses. Christmas in Japan meant dates and desserts and reservations you had to fight for; it meant music too cheerful for how cold it actually was. In here, it meant a kettle ticking itself quiet and the smell of tea seeping into the steam, and Bakugou sitting on the counter with both hands around a chipped mug like he was trying to warm his knuckles from the inside out.He wasn’t the most knowledgeable when it came to sex. He’d had it—yeah, multiple times; he was an adult and he didn’t flinch from the word—but “knowing” wasn’t the point anyone kept pretending it was. Kirishima was the one who read, who asked questions out loud, who turned things into conversations without making them weird. Bakugou learned by doing, by paying attention, by not bullshitting himself about what worked and what didn’t. Somewhere in the middle of all that, he’d put a name to something he already knew: demisexual. He didn’t care about labels as a sport; he cared about being accurate. It meant that his brain didn’t flip for strangers, didn’t spark at passing faces, didn’t light for anyone who wasn’t Kirishima. It never had, not once. Even back when it would’ve been easier if it did.He could trace it in a straight line if he wanted to. The stupid friends-with-benefits thing that wasn’t stupid at all because nothing about Kirishima was halfway; how they’d moved like they were solving a problem together and then kept moving because stopping would’ve meant admitting it was already more than sex. He’d told himself it was practical. He’d told himself it was release. Then he’d listened to the way his own voice sounded when he said Kirishima’s name and realised he was full of shit. Attraction hadn’t fallen on him like a lightning bolt; it had built itself one brick at a time: fights survived, meals shared, the space beside him on a couch, the way the room calibrated when Kirishima walked into it. By the time he said it out loud—even if it wasn’t the first time he felt it—it was already the most obvious thing in the world. He loved him. Everyone else could get in line behind that.Steam laced the window. He should’ve wiped it with his sleeve, but he liked the smear of color it made on the street. Red. White. Taxi headlights cutting through like a blade. He lifted the mug and let the heat hit the skin under his nose, the bitter edge of the tea grounding enough to keep his brain from sprinting ahead of him. They were supposed to leave for a party later—Mina’s idea, obviously. Mina’s parties were like small natural disasters: predicted, stubborn, somehow cheerful even when they knocked the power out. The last one had turned into a legend that would apparently haunt him until he was eighty. He wasn’t interested in repeating it. He wasn’t interested in listening to Kaminari call him “a shrub” again either. The group chat had gotten creative. He’d pretended to mute it. He hadn’t.“Winter sale,” Mina had said, months ago, kneeling on an office chair backwards with a marker clenched in her teeth and a spreadsheet open on every screen they owned. “Think about it: drop a small run, get people in the habit of checking weekly, make the restock a game. We’ll call it ‘Ignition: Bright Season.’”“Bright Season is fucking stupid,” he’d told her. “Also, too many vowels.”“Fine,” she’d said, unbothered. “Your brand, your vowels, but trust me on the timing.”He did trust her. The sale had gone live, and the Ignition warehouse had turned into a wind tunnel of cardboard and tape guns, and a week later, they were watching the numbers climb with their hands on their heads like they’d just pulled off a rescue in under five minutes. Ignition had started as a PR move, a way to get people to actually like him. Now it was a machine with a heartbeat. Photoshoots, drops, the way a good jacket could make a kid stand up straighter in a mirror. It was stupid that cloth could do that, and true anyway.He glanced down at the mug—white letters over orange, the logo clean and mean against ceramic—and let his mouth twist. He’d fought for those lines. He’d fought for everything. Ground Zero, his hero agency, hadn’t been the result of a handshake; it was a blueprint he’d redrawn six times until it stopped wobbling under his feet. He’d learned to hire people who’d call him on his bullshit. He’d learned that delegation wasn’t surrender and that a “no” didn’t mean the whole building fell. The interns were fast, the ops team knew what a deadline was, and the rescue board in the bullpen looked like a wall of quiet victories: names, coordinates, the word cleared written with confidence. People sent letters. Parents

Derek had come to terms with the fact that the horrific tragedy of his family (biological, that is) was not his fault a little while ago. If someone insisted on asking for a specific timeframe…a year, maybe. He’d been healing from it for much longer than that by this point, but finally realizing that it truly was not his fault, that he had been a pawn in an evil game and not the chess master? Being able to think about his parents, his cousins, his little siblings, without drowning in guilt? A good, solid year, he would say.
Right now, that was a damn good thing too.
If he had anticipated anyone calling him again from Beacon Hills after the final showdown with the hunters, it would have been Scott. They still traded texts every few months, just to check in. A phone call would have been cause for concern, but not entirely unexpected if something new was going down. And it likely would have just been for any advice Derek might have had. Scott wouldn’t call him back to Beacon Hills unless it was dire, just because that’s who Scott had become. A strong, confident Alpha of his pack, who was considerate enough of Derek’s history with the town not to try to drag him back if it wasn’t completely necessary. Though Derek would have gone anyway most likely. He wouldn’t mind.
However, the call he did get was much more worrying.
“Sheriff? Is everything alright?”
“Derek, how are you?” The voice on the other end was warm, friendly, as though it hadn’t been nearing two and a half years since they had spoken. If it had been anyone else, the alarm bells would have been going off in Derek’s head. Sheriff Stilinski was a no-nonsense kind of man, much like his son (and Derek felt a stab of…something, for a moment, before he refocused). If something bad was happening, he would open with it directly. So Derek, while certain there was a reason for this unexpected call, calmed down slightly.
“I’m doing well, sir,” he responded. “It’s good to hear from you.”
The sheriff laughed. “You may not think so after this.”
Oh. Damn.
“Is Stiles okay? I mean, is he – who’s hurt? I can come, I can be there by tomorrow—”
More laughter, then a soothing, “No one’s hurt, Derek. I’m sorry, I should have led with that. Stiles is fine, everyone’s fine.”
Derek sighed in relief. “Oh. Then…what’s wrong?” Because despite everything, Derek had always quite liked Sheriff Stilinski, and couldn’t imagine a situation outside of an emergency where he wouldn’t mind hearing from him once in awhile.
“Well, I have a friend who’s part of the EMS department in Sacramento,” the sheriff said, “and he called me because they’re looking for you. Apparently, they have something of yours…” The sheriff kept talking, and Derek kept listening, and by the time the phone call ended, the next flight to Sacramento was booked and he had plans to meet Sheriff Stilinski (“Noah, call me Noah, son,” Derek was told) at UC Davis Medical Center the next day.
***
Derek stared down at the little hospital crib, only half-listening to the firefighter and doctor explaining what had happened. How Sacramento had implemented a safe, easy way for unfit or unready parents to give up their child anonymously, with the promise that they were off the hook and the baby would be found in a timely manner. Most of the time, babies were left with the clothes on their backs and maybe wrapped in a blanket. This one, however, came with a note. The note had two names – the baby’s and Derek’s.
The firefighter who’d found him miraculously recognized Derek’s name, and after following procedure, contacted Noah Stilinski to see if he knew of the whereabouts of the supposed father of this child. So now, Derek was here, still unable to believe his eyes despite the evidence cooing in front of him. A soft, squishy, three week old baby with a shock of dark hair and Derek’s nose.
By now, the doctor had stepped in to offer DNA testing to confirm that the child was Derek’s and to figure out who the mother was as well. Because apparently, in this case, she had forfeited her right to remain anonymous by naming the supposed father. If Derek wanted to go after her for custody or child support, he legally could.
“I don’t need a DNA test,” Derek heard himself say faintly. He didn’t. When Tim embarked on a mission that necessitated sneaking into a fancy party as Caroline Hill, he thought he’d been prepared for anything. Man-Bats. Two-Face. Poison Ivy. Caroline faces the man and smiles. “That depends. I also wrote it at a time I was overthinking about specific things that day and the day before so I had planned out a lot of the poem in my head when I was supposed to be sleeping. I struggle a lot with feeling guilty in my relationship because of my mental health burdens and also having moved schools, now I'm not able to support them physically nearly as much. I don't think I'm ever going to be able to get used to being at different schools but I might write a seperate poem on that. I also overthink how I feel like I can't support my partner enough because of my own struggles and I feel too needy towards them. I generally just struggle with feeling like they deserve someone better than me, probably because of a combination of reasons relating to my own mental health and it gets especially bad when I don't get to see them every weekend. The poem itself describes my feelings of self-doubt because of overthinking and also feeling like my support is never enough for my partner through using organs as an analogy, representing the raw-ness and disconnect I feel when I'm overthinking about our relationship. Clinging onto your heart,
Your heart that’s beating for me

The responsibility you’ve trusted me with
Your unconditional love
Shouldn’t be with someone like meEvery day that I spend at school
Thinking about what you’d be doing
Drains me of my blood,
My energy

Your thoughts don’t spiral like mine,

Next to you,
offering their heart in exchange for yours

One afternoon when you met Mycroft after a mission, before you could start to report he asked if you minded joining him for tea. On the other hand, when you did meet him, the conversations were longer and his company was more pleasant than you ever thought it could be.
Which still didn’t answer how you got in that situation, you never saw it coming. Do you like his company? Yes. Do you enjoy talking to him? Yes. Do you have stronger feelings for him? Hell no! Then why did you do that? He sure regretted it, didn’t he? How would you look in his face now?
The feeling that Mycroft would enter his bedroom at any minute grew inside of you, making you apprehensive, so you decided to get up already, make the bed as quickly as possible and try to sneak out of his house so you didn’t have to deal with this situation.
As you gathered your clothes and made the bed, images of the night prior started popping on your mind again, against your will. A planet as common as every other one and with a name just as common at least in it’s inhabitants tongue, Wer’huja. It orbited around a young yellow Sun and in return it had three small Moons orbiting around it. It’s surface was mostly covered with plains of red dirt where it’s inhabitants made their civilizations and lakes of gigantic dimensions wich gave the water their cities ran on.

The vision boxes and the radio signals traveled with that news and got it to every tribe and clan wich made up their nations. Claws rose up to the sky in defiance, eye-stalks closed from fear, and the carcasses and shells of the more sad of their kind piled up under where they let themselves fall.
The star soon arrived at their planet, but it wasn’t a star at all! An odd being bathed in orange fire descended from the sky. It had an odd shape and an even odder voice. It asked about their planet and it’s name and so their Dirtologist told it what they knew from their study of the worlds sediment. The being content with the answer nodded it’s head and flew upwards to the sky once again.
The next day the burning creature flew down to meet them and asked them about themselves, their clans and their customs so the Culturians told it about the history of their many clans and their stupid wars of old. They told it about their days of joy and the moments when they must seek peace with each other. They told it the name they had given themselves, Ishkant’hees. The most brave of them dared to play a folk song of theirs to the creature and the creature flew down and motioned to hold the instrument and the flames in it’s own soft claws went out and upwards it flew once again with the instrument.
The day after that the creature flew down again and asked about their technology. Their Thinkers and Tinkerers showed it the many advances their civilization had created, their most pridefull creation a small metalic helper wich could be configurated to help anywhere and anywhen. The creature looked longinly at the bronce colored helper but let it down on the ground as it flew upwards yet again.
Several days after went by befire the creature came down again so the next time it did clans upon clans came to see it and hear what it would ask them. It said “There’s nothing more of Science or Culture for me to ask of you. May I ask then about each of you?” And so the Ishkant’hees lines up one behind another and one by one they told the cretaure their names and what they did. The hatchlings that were allowed to speak with it spoke about their broodmates and the joyfull nothing that only the young can tell.
One of the many Astrosophists wich had seen the creature arrive was the last to speak with it. “May I be so bold as to ask you?” They said. “Many stars have gone out, I’ve seen. And with them many planets. Where you from any of those that you always look sad when asking questions about ours?”
“No, not from those planets.” The creature said.
As the two of them finished their chat the creature looked even sadder as it flew it’s final flight upwards.
“What is your name!?” A small hatchling yelled before the creature could escape their sight. The creature looked unconfortable as it looked deep in thought. An odd name it had, but they couldn’t expect anything else from such an odd creature. Yon’hee… absolutely odd indeed.
Several days passed and Yon’hee wouldn’t come down again and most of them thought it would soon leave their planet behind. Their celestial machines flared up suddenly and Yon’nee could be seen flying at great speeds around their world and as it did they saw how it’s flames changed from it’s usual orange to a silver color.

“I herald his begining. I… I-I herald your end. I herald…”
“…Galactus.”

Nozomi wakes up feeling groggy.She's always liked napping, but lately, it feels like she's been sleeping for whole days at a time. She barely even remembers going to work, or... even leaving the house.Not her house, though. Nico's house. She's in Nico's house right now. Of course, that's normal, she reminds herself, but for some reason, it still disorientates her, as if she wasn't expecting it.She absently runs her finger along the glowing runes on her shoulder. Even they seem odd to her. Perhaps she was just having a weird dream, and her sense of normality is all out of whack.Still feeling a little dazed, she wanders towards the sound of cooking. When she peeks into the kitchen, she sees Nico working on... is that dinner?"What time is it?" she mumbles.Nico looks up from her pots and starts a little. "Nozomi?" she says. "Did you wake up again?"Again? How many naps has Nozomi taken today? She can't even remember.Still, she does her best to put on a sly smile and tease Nico a little."That's what happens when you take a nap, Niccochi," she says. "You wake up at the end of it.""A nap. Right." For some reason, Nico smirks a little.Nozomi frowns slightly, rubbing her head. Something feels off, and she can't quite figure it out. Her thoughts are still cloudy...."Why don't you go back to sleep?" Nico says."What?" Nozomi says. "I think I've slept plenty...""Don't say that," Nico says. "You're still tired, aren't you? Vaguely, she wonders why it doesn't seem that important to actually go lie down, but Nico doesn't seem concerned. If Nico thinks it's fine, it must be fine...Nozomi's eyes close, and she slips back into the dream.In the dream, she stands naked in Nico's kitchen. The runes of control across her body pulse gently as her eyes open again, this time clouded, and the worry vanishes from her face, replaced with a serene and happy smile.Nico lets out a sigh of relief and reaches up to stroke Nozomi's cheek affectionately."You know, sometimes I wonder if you sabotaged your notes on purpose," she says. "Considering how patchy the runes are..."She shrugs. "Well, I suppose you just hadn't finished yet. If they were perfected, you would have already used them on me, right?"Nozomi nods. In the dream, that all makes sense. She even remembers researching the runes, in a far away time when the dream didn't exist."Good thing a little idol magic was the secret ingredient," Nico says, winking. "After all, if you didn't love Nico so much, these patchy runes wouldn't even manage to keep you under as much as they do, right?""Right," Nozomi says cheerfully. "But you figured out to use the runes of desire to amplify the runes of control.""I did, didn't I?" Nico says proudly. "Well, what else can you expect from the world's greatest idol? Maybe I'm a genius of magic as well as smiles.""Your pots, mistress," Nozomi says patiently, and Nico quickly turns, stirring and seasoning as she turns down one of the flames."Hug me," she says, not looking at Nozomi. "But make sure not to get in the way.""Yes, mistress," Nozomi says. She wraps her arms gently around Nico, trying to avoid restricting the motion of Nico's arms. Nico leans back happily into her as she continues to cook."Dinner will be finished soon," she says. "Make sure to eat a lot of Nico's delicious cooking, okay? You're going to need that energy tonight.""Yes, mistress," Nozomi says.Her mind settles down in a restful state as she stands absently, waiting for her next order.It's a very peaceful dream that she's having. A dream where she's Nico's prize in a contest of sorcery against the Nozomi of the past. A dream where she spends most of her days in a blissful state of trance, serving and loving Nico, interrupted only by brief periods of confusion as the magic splutters and falters.It's a happy dream. As Nozomi cuddles closer to Nico, she decides that if this is what she's going to dream...Why even try to wake up?

It happened at lunch one day.
Forte Keys is waiting on the lunch line when she feels someone... looking at her. Turning her head, she sees a pink-haired girl with ridiculous hair. She’s staring at Keys expectantly, but her expression is faintly... puzzled? And a little sad. She holds a lunch tray in her hands, like she got distracted on the way back to her usual seat. Upon making eye contact, the girl steps a little closer and talks.“You look exactly like someone I kind of... don’t... know,” She says, hesitantly. “Sorry. Is that weird? That was really weird. Uh... Bye!” She scurries off, dropping plastic fork on the way.“Wait... I think I...” Know exactly what you mean, Keys starts to respond, but the strange girl is already gone.
She states after her for a beat, trying to place how this girl she’s never seen before struck some kind of familiar chord. Keys feels a tap on her shoulder. “Excuse me, the line’s moved,” a red-haired girl behind her says.
“My apologies,” Keys responds, and moves forward.
“Hey, Lindsay? You missed your entrance like, three times. Are you okay?”It’s after school and Team Forte is refining a new song for their next album. Roni, thankfully, has all the parts figured out on this one -- a sugary song about young love -- but Keys is being more of a hindrance than she realized.“Oh? Yes,” Keys responds, after a moment. “I’m fine.”Debbi and Roni exchange a look.“Hey...” Roni rests her hand on Lindsay’s shoulder. “If you need to talk about something, you know you can tell us, right? That’s why we’re friends.”Lindsay holds her gaze for a second, before receding into herself, with that elusive, stoic-but-pretty air she cultivates so well. Roni is an excellent leader; there will never be any contest about the fluidity of their team, as long as Roni is running it.Keys sighs. “Alright.” And she regales them the events of a few days ago, where a pink-haired girl seemed to have known her before.It’s only Debbi who manages to come up with something to say. “That’s... weird.”Are you sure it wasn’t just nervousness from a fan? Gail signs.Debbi signs back, how do you know she’s a fan?Lindsay shakes her head. “I’ve never seen her before. But... I think I know what she means, somehow.” She adjusts in her seat. “Then, and since, looking at her... I feel like... we’ve avoided something awful,” she says, sotto voche.
