Lilith loved putting her head in Azura’s lap. Her thighs were firm, yet made a soft resting place. She admired the scent of the perfume her wife wore as well as that of Azura herself, and she never forgot the fact that she alone was lucky enough to be so close to Azura that she knew what she smelled like. One leg was clad in white silk; the other she left bare, but to Lilith, her skin was more delicate than any satin. She loved the brush of Azura’s hands in her hair, the whispered song of her voice, and peering up to see her gentle, serene face. Every night on which Azura was in the mood for lovemaking, as a sort of thanks for the gift of being able to rest her head in her lap, Lilith gave her sweet kisses from her lips down to her toes, moved up to her smooth thighs, and pleasured her.She loved it when Azura put her head in her lap, too. When she’d first done it, Azura had shyly asked if it was all right, blushing in the most darling way, though she should have known there was nothing Lilith would deny her. But once she’d gotten settled in with her eyes closed and Lilith had begun to alternate between combing her hair with her hands and peppering her cute nose, long lashes, and lips with kisses, she had breathed contented, almost sleepy sighs. Shifting against her, she sometimes whispered, “You’re as soft as a cloud and as warm as sunshine.” Now and again she took gentle hold of Lilith’s hands and drew them around to lay them on her heart.Lilith adored sitting or curling up in her wife’s lap while in dragon form. She fit so well there. Azura seemed to agree. She gave the sweetest giggles when dragon-Lilith hopped eagerly into her lap and when she closed her eyes beneath the pets Azura gave her head. What Lilith loved best was when Azura, while stroking her head, began to sing to her.The embraces they shared were heavenly in their warmth, and every night they spent together was magical. Azura’s smiles were more radiant than the moon. Yet at times she became somber and quiet. This afternoon was one of those times.
They went out for a stroll by the ocean and stopped to gaze out at the shimmering water. But, after a while, Azura’s expression had changed, reflecting a hint of pensiveness instead of the happy contentment she’d radiated before. Lilith moved closer to her.“Azura, love?. . .Are you all right?” She laid a hand on hers. “What’s on your mind, angel?”Azura was silent for a few moments, and then: “I’m fine, sweetest. It’s just that. . .the war is over, I’ve found so much happiness with you, with my family. . .and yet sometimes it’s hard to fully enjoy it when I remember that there are people who aren’t nearly as fortunate as I am. I wish that I had all the power in the world and could be everywhere at once so that I could. . .” She trailed off here, and when she continued to gaze off across the ocean, Lilith knew she was thinking of people on the other side of the sea whom she couldn’t hold close and protect.Lilith’s heart ached. She had always wanted peace for humanity, but had never dared hope to be strong enough, useful enough to protect many people other than the ones closest to her. “I understand,” she whispered. “If one person - even one man, woman or child - hurts, we should all hurt, because all people are equally precious.”Azura turned to look at her with those gentle, beautiful golden lakes for eyes. She held out a gloved hand for her. Lilith came over to sit in her wife’s lap. Her bonnet was gently removed, and as her hair was stroked, Azura murmured, 
“I want to live to see world peace and happiness.”Lilith leaned into her touch. “You will, dearest. Don’t give up on that dream just yet. Once we were both frail, scared little girls, but we grew strong enough to fight for what we believed in, and I’ve found a happiness I never thought I’d live to see. I believe there’s no limit to what we can accomplish if we try our hardest. Let’s travel the world together and make things right a little bit at a time.”Azura kissed her cheek, then brought her own cheek to rest against Lilith’s. Lilith could feel that she was smiling. She decided to do something she knew Azura liked alot and took on her dragon form. This got a soft giggle out of Azura. Putting her arms around Lilith, she pressed kisses like dew-drops to her head until she blushed. Lilith settled down happily in her lap.Yes. . .we’ll let the ocean lead us and heal the world’s hurts together. I know we will. There’s nothing I can’t do without the love of my life at my side.

“So you'll meet me at that cafe later, right?”
“Mhm, the one near campus, I presume.”
“Cool, I'll see you there, Rayne.”
As fall exams were rolling in, so did the stress and need for studying. Rayne went down to the closest cafe from her college to study with her friends, hoping that she’d see them there. Unfortunately, upon arrival she sees a cafe packed with other students trying to squeeze a few hours of study time in, and not a single one of them that looks like her friends.
“Did they bail on me or something..?” Rayne thought to herself.
She nervously slinked into the line, still wondering while waiting to order. “Maybe they’re just late, yeah.. They wouldn’t randomly just.. Fuck”
Rayne’s train of thought is interrupted when she hears the server ask for her order.
“Um, I’ll get an ube latte and chocolate croissant, please”
“Alright just pay here and take a seat while we prepare your order”, the server gestures to the card machine as Rayne pulls out her card.
She quickly pays using her card and tries to find an empty table. But with little to no prevail as a result.
“Since when did this many college students decide to study at night?” She mumbles to herself. Fortunately, Rayne finally spots a table with only one person, one woman to be exact.
But, something was off about her.
She had extremely pale skin and deadpan eyes with a soulless stare. Maybe she was just goth, I mean she dresses that way, Rayne thought to herself.
Rayne’s thoughts were quickly interrupted by the woman asking if she had nowhere to sit. Her stomach churned, but ultimately sat down at the unattended seat in front of her.
“Um… thank you, uh, I’ll go get my order, be right back..”
The woman's expression doesn’t change, but simply nods in acknowledgement and looks back down at her assignments.
Rayne gets up and walks to the pick up counter and receives her latte and croissant.
“Thank you,” Rayne says before she walks back to her table.
Once she gets back to her seat, she looks at the mysterious woman and wants to get to know her. Maybe just her name at least.
“What’s um, your name?”
She blankly stares at Rayne and takes a few seconds to answer, “...Lilith”
“Wow, that’s a really pretty name, I’m Rayne.”
Rayne reaches out her hand, hoping from a handshake but just getting another dead stare in response from Lilith, almost as if she didn’t know what a social cue was.
Rayne awkwardly pushed her curls out of her face, pulled back her hand and sat back down, searching through her bag she got out her papers, notebooks, and other miscellaneous notes. She figured that she may be able to try to have a conversation with her again.
“Well, do you have anything you’re studying for?”
Lilith stares at her with silence again, before saying, “Just reviewing some notes, but I’m usually caught up with everything.”
This makes Rayne pique with curiosity, “So, what do you major in then? I’m in the medical field.”
“..Fine arts,” Lilith responds shyly.
“Oh, nice! That sounds like a fun major, assuming that you’re an artist.”
Rayne looks over her supplies and sees a notebook opened to a few drawings that look like a detailed anatomy study. It seemed smudged with a bunch of notes every ‘study: hands, feet, noses’,
“...Well, it's more stressful than it looks, if something looks wrong, I’ve gotta redo it, erase, redraw, study…”
Lilith starts to rant on about how much drawing “sucks”, the way no one seemed to understand the struggle with it, and how hard it is. Rayne doesn’t mind though, she liked hearing Lilith rant, maybe just hearing her talk was something she enjoyed.
Lilith had a sweet voice, nasally, but still sweet. Maybe the fact that her voice sounded like that made her kind of cute.
“Oh, I’m ranting aren’t I? I…I’ll stop, we’ve both gotta study, well I mean you do. I just have to review some things… ”
“No, it’s fine一”
“No, really I’ve got quite a problem with ranting, people tell me all the time…”
“Lilith一”
“Huh?”
“You’re ranting again..”
Rayne couldn’t help but smile, and laugh a little.
“Wait一 I’m not laughing you, I just… uh sorry, I’ll just let you study.”
Lilith returns the smile and returns back to her notes, with a faint shade of pink behind her ears.
A few minutes later, Rayne slides a small piece of paper towards Lilith. “It’s just my number, if you want to meet up and talk again after today.”
“Ah, well, do you have classes tomorrow? Maybe we can meet back here after class if you’d like,” Lilith replies.
Rayne gives her a thumbs up and they both set a meeting time in the late afternoon, taking note for the future that Lilith isn’t a morning person. The sounds of rustling and people leaving the cafe fill their ears. Lilith starts to pack up her own materials as well. “It’s been fun talking with you, see you then.”
Rayne gives her a wave goodbye and chooses to stay longer to finish her work, contemplating on whether or not she should bring conversation cards the next day or not.

Viper doesn’t like personal relationships between her agents, so the fact that she has found herself involved with one of her agents makes her feel like nothing short of a hypocrite. In her defense, she didn’t intend to accept (nevertheless ever reciprocate) Chamber’s advances, but sometimes life works in mysterious ways that benefit her sometimes she’s a weak woman who gives into the charm of insistent men.Life also works in mysterious ways that do her more harm than good, because she’s spent her entire day wondering why everything is so quiet. It it already half past twelve, and by now, her human dog (as KJ has decided to call him) would be here, handing her a plate of whatever there is for lunch with a kiss that she would be trying to avoid like the plague (because her otherwise sterile lab is not a place for things like these) and entertain her with a ‘brief’ conversation that will inevitably extend for as long as she can allow him to distract her from her work.
Today, however, she finds herself alone, sitting in front of a vial filled with a green viscous liquid
 that she’s considering pouring over a piece of paper (to make sure it can’t spark a fire), staring at the clock with her peripheral vision. She lets the time tick by, growing restless after a while. She tries to convince herself she’s simply hungry (despite knowing that she has never had much of an appetite), but when the clock marks two, she has officially lost the little patience she had.
“Waiting for your dog?” Killjoy asks eventually, after watching her tap the floor with her foot for a good two minutes.
“Shut up,” She demands, glaring at her. Killjoy rolls her eyes, more than used to her antics.
“You’ve been antsy for two hours,” she replies. “You’re waiting for him, aren’t you?”
“Don’t you have work to do?” Viper asks her, staring at the computer Killjoy is supposed to be cleaning.
“I’m just saying,” she says, shrugging. “If you want to take your lunch break, I can be trusted on my own,”
Viper narrows her eyes at her, aware of what she’s trying to imply. She looks at her current object of interest again, staring at the green liquid inside the glass. She knows Killjoy can be trusted around her equipment; actually, if she were to trust anyone around her things, it would certainly be the little mouse, but she is still unsure. Even if she decided to use her lunch break looking for him, she wouldn’t know where to check.
She sighs, running a hand through her hair and ditching her mask momentarily.

He clicked his tongue, eyeing the cake that seemed to just stare at him back despite knowing that was ridiculous. With a scoff he pushed his chair back and got out of his cubicle, his workmate has not come back yet and knowing him he wasn't going to for another 30 mins or so.
He passed by the birthday guy, a skeleton who seemed way too happy to be chatting with the rest.
Jay didn't know them too well and honestly he was too bothered on learning either, instead he just waved at the them not really caring if he was seen or not.
Instead he just kept walking away from the commotion.
He wandered for a bit, drowning the outside world until he reached one of the pillars close to the individual offices before standing and leaned against.
He could still hear the party.
Out of his pocket he got a cigarette
and a lighter.
Slumping against the pillar he sighed before bringing the cigarette
to his mouth and exhaling some smoke.
He hated parties, for whatever reason seeing the people so happy, cheerful just made him… hurt.
He felt a void inside him he couldn't describe accompanied by a sense of longing, for what? He couldn't tell.
Maybe he wished to have what they had, not necessarily a party but-
He couldn't even properly remember his Birthday.
It was quite funny and sad, he could remember his name and yet everything else escaped him and despite all there were times when emotions would made themselves known, emotions he couldn't place nor explain.
He found out it was easier to walk away from them.
He finished his cigarette
slowly, making sure to drag his break as long as possible until he found himself numb enough to continue working.
As he walked back and noticed the commotion had died down he wondered how much more he could take.
He had heard of other positions being opened in other sectors, maybe he could get one where he had to deal with less people directly.
Finally he reached his office again, noticing the cubicle still empty and walked towards his desk.
Once he sat down he was greeted with the cake once again, plain white with uneven, melting frosting, exactly what you would expect from a cake from your work.
With a sigh and an annoyed murmur he took the sticky paper plate, grimacing at the feeling feeling before turning, walking across the room and leaving the cake on the other unoccupied desk before walking out towards the bathrooms.
He wasn't hungry anyways.

Felix loved his mother. Every morning at church, they’d join hands and pray. On their knees, on the hard wooden floor, they would stay until it bruised, until his knees were sore and achy. The floor smelled faintly of varnish and incense, a sharp, bitter scent that burned his nose after long hours of kneeling. Sunlight slanted through the stained-glass windows, painting fractured rainbows across their bowed heads, but even the beauty of color could not soften the ache in his knees.“Jesus,” his mother would say, “is the key to our hearts. Only if you’ve sinned before would He allow the pain to hold. So you must pray. And pray.”She would watch the bruises form on her baby darling’s knees and convince herself that Jesus wanted this. Jesus will prove my child’s redemption, she told herself. Etiquette. Silence. The quiet was heavy, like a blanket of lead pressing down on the wooden pews, broken only by the occasional creak of a board or the soft whimper of Felix shifting under the pain.One night, while polishing her cross, she turned down the volume on her Christian-specific channels and listened for Felix. Silence. She moved upstairs and found her baby boy drawing and scribbling quietly. The soft glow of the lamp made the shadows dance across the walls, turning the corners of the room into black hollows that seemed to breathe.“My dear, may I see the drawing?” she asked softly, her voice a whisper that seemed swallowed by the shadows.Felix whispered back, but only then did he notice her. His poor, lost eight-year-old eyes held up a picture: her, with all three of her crosses, the lines heavy and uneven, and a small figure in red crouched in the corner, smiling faintly.“My dear, who is that?” she asked again, barely above a whisper.“Mommy, it’s my friend.”Her eyes widened. At first, she seemed almost ecstatic—but then horror overtook her. She screamed, a high, splintering sound, and tore the paper to shreds. The pieces floated to the floor, settling like brittle leaves in autumn. Felix shivered at the sound, each tear echoing through the room like distant thunder.Now, in case you didn’t know, Felix’s mother was extremely religious. She would have dreams of spirits representing the Holy Trinity, pale and ethereal, whispering secrets of devotion and sacrifice. Their whispers slithered into her mind, curling like smoke around her thoughts, and she would obey.One night, she heard a whisper: Go bring me a live lamb. Without hesitation, she spent nearly three hundred dollars on the freshest, purest baby lamb she could find in New Jersey.Little Felix awoke in his pajamas to the guttural screams of the lamb as his mother dissected it. His pajamas, stitched by her hands with verses and prayers, glimmered faintly in the moonlight spilling through the window, the fabric seeming almost alive under the silver rays.“Mommy?” he whispered, his small voice quivering.He was cut off by another guttural roar from the lamb. Felix pressed his face into the quilt, feeling the rough weave against his cheek. The coppery scent of blood seeped through the cracks under the door, mingling with the faint perfume his mother always wore, a sickly-sweet scent that made his stomach churn.He thought of running, but the hallway stretched endlessly in the dark, shadows twisting like living things across the floorboards. Each creak of the boards under his mother’s movements made his chest tighten. The room felt smaller, suffocating, as if the walls themselves leaned inward, watching.He decided to go back to bed, curling under the quilt. The verses his mother sewn onto the pajamas itched terribly, for she was not the greatest seamstress. He drifted slowly, in and out of consciousness before finally closing his small, purple eyelids. And falling asleep.

Maron hears the news secondhand. Thirdhand. Fourth or fifth.It starts with a pounding on the door. Gaspard hurries to answer it just the same as always, walking with all his weight on his heels, a mighty clunk-clack against the entry flooring. He opens the door, pales, and calls for the master of the house.General de Jarjayes hears the news right there in the entry hall, in front of the staircase, and Maron hears him from her room—the sound of his grief a strangled cry.She knows the truth of it immediately and feels helpless to do anything but sit and wait patiently for the news to reach her—to be the last one who matters to know of it, save the master’s other children. But that is the way of things, being what she is to this family.An hour later, she hears it from Madame, who bore the order to march quietly but cannot do the same with her anguish. Maron knows, already, that one or both children are lost, but chokes on the news, anyway, just as her master did. Tears well up and tip over as she bows her head.Both.“Shot,” Madame says, trembling like an aspen in the wind. “Only a day apart. André and then Oscar.” Her voice cracks on her youngest daughter’s name and she buries her face against Maron’s shoulder.Maron holds her tight, her own tears falling into Madame’s hair, and wonders how it happened. What their wounds looked like and where they were located. How quickly they slipped away from this life and left it for another.“Of course they would go together,” Madame says when she straightens.Maron reaches for her handkerchief and presses it to her stinging nose, nodding. “They’ve always done everything together,” she agrees.The knowledge serves as some small solace for a moment as they look at one another. It’s a tiny anchor—not enough to secure the boat in the raging storm—but better than nothing.Madame’s mouth moves then, as if to speak, but it takes her a long time to do so.“The children,” she finally manages, handkerchief pressed to her face as if to hide it, the words tearing out of her throat like a wail. “They can’t be brought home.”Even if the master wants them returned to see them buried, and surely that is the case, he can’t allow it. They are both traitors to the crown; he cannot lay claim to either of them.She nods because there is nothing else to do.
Later, when Maron is alone, the long grief settles over her like a shroud.She closes her eyes and thinks of André. The orphaned little boy she found in Arras waiting for her. She remembers seeing her daughter in him, that first day, in his dark hair and eyes and the tears that slid down the curve of his round face, but he proved he was his own person in the years that followed: his quick, easy smiles, the way his tongue often poked out of his mouth when he was trying to concentrate, his posture as he sat to listen to Oscar play the violin, chin resting against the back of his hand.She misses him already, that boy who sat with her in the carriage and looked out the window, tugging at his stiff neckcloth—and the man who dined with her the night before he marched into Paris, voice calm and reassuring despite his clumsy handling of the meal.She thinks of Oscar, next. The wailing infant she held in her arms to present to the master: a beautiful child who ended up being too smart for her own good. That smug grin that exploded across her face every time she got her way and shouldn’t have. The colonel facing off against André in the yard, laughing, and the brigadier-general standing at attention, hoping as always for her father’s approval. The woman, shy and hiding it behind barbs and complaints, who stepped out in front of everyone in a gown. Off to a dance and then back again to drown herself in strong spirits day and night. The sound of her pushing her glass away without filling it.She misses her, too, that girl who couldn’t sit still at the kitchen table, even to eat a snack—and the woman who promised to return to tell her those words one more time…How did they go again?“I love you, Nanny. I always will. For all time.”Strange that she can almost hear them, here, in the deafening silence of her room.

Silence. The creaking of wood. The patter of rain. The absence of sound. The absence of him.
It was deafening to the boy sat in the barn, his back to the couch, knees brought up to his chest. The absence of sound was a reminder of what he lost, of what he caused.
He hadn't talked in over a week now. Hadn't spoken a word. It wasn't for lack of want, he just had nothing to say. Lana had approached him multiple times, the woman who's meant to be the love of his life. She tried to comfort him but her presence just drove the knife even deeper. Her presence was just a reminder.
His mother had attempted. Her face was gaunt, hair ashen with grief, and eyes red raw from tears. When Clark laid eyes on her there were no words to even begin to encompass how sorry he was. How can you even start to apologize for taking away the love of your mothers life?
Chloe attempted every day. She would come up to the barn, sit cross legged next to him with a plate of food and just talk about nonsensical things. He would listen. He appreciated that she was filling the silence with noise. It was distracting.
But it still hurt. And he still had nothing to say.
Not only was he at a loss for discussion points, but on the fifth day of his stay up in the loft, he had enough of being void of emotion.
He couldn't feel anything, he was numb. He had killed a man. His own father. He wanted to feel something. Anger, rage, sadness, guilt, pain. Anything. So he had walked over to the lead box in the drawer and opened it.
He sat far enough away that the effects wouldn't kill him, but still close enough that there was a hum of pain. He found it peaceful. A reminder. Turning his emotional pain into a physical one.

Angel stood in the middle of his bedroom, the floor was littered with discarded clothes of every shape, size, and color. Pants scattered recklessly, dresses too short for a fancy dinner, and somehow a sock that managed to get stuck to the ceiling, was evidence enough of a struggle. 
“How do I have all these clothes and still nothing to wear?!” Angel asked to no one but himself in frustration. Quick flashes of clothes being flung across the room gave the allusion of a battlefield in the midst of a war. 
Maybe it was his mind racing, or his nerves or the alcohol he drank to calm himself but it had completely slipped his mind to pick out an outfit before hand. 
“It’s just a date…” he muttered, yanking a sweater over his head before realizing it was inside out. Off it went again. “With Husk, what could go wrong…” Angel laughed bitterly, looking to his left at the clock on his nightstand accusingly: 6:48. He need to be down in the lobby by 7. 
Angel took a moment to look around, truly look around at what he had, then he saw it. A simple black dress shoved in the back of the closet. It was perfect for the occasion though a little bit plain. To make it more stylized, Angel hurriedly threw on a waist belt made up of tiny heart that jingled every time he moved and thick black leather platform shoes decorated with silver rhinestoned hearts, hopping on one foot when he couldn’t get the shoes on quick enough. Classy white gloves and makeup was haphazardly thrown into his bag without a second thought. 
As he sped out the door, only barely remembering to grab his purse, all he could think about was how extremely late he was. Angel would probably get a light scolding later from Husk about punctuality. 
But as Angel made his way down one of the staircase, he looked over to see his gambler of a partner doing the same. Husk must have felt the staring as he slowly looked up to see his pink haired partner doing the same thing as him. 
Their paces slowed as the made they way towards each other both seemingly aware of the moment they’ve caught themselves in. Once in the middle lobby, they stopped, standing just a few feet apart, looking as if wanting to say something. 
“I didn’t know what to wear..” Both men blurted out in unison. For a moment, all they could do was stare at each other in surprise. Then, without warning, they burst out laughing. It was awkward and loving, but in the best way. 
“I got these for you, Legs” Husk finally catching his breath long enough to speak. Angel couldn’t tell if it was from the laughing or the cat’s nerves but the shaking of the tightly gripped flowers was obviously, though Angel would never ruin Husk’s illusion. 
Angel reached out for them, brushing his hands against Husk’s as he picked up the flowers to admire them. Roses, but each and every one of them was a different shade of pink or red. 
Angel’s heart could do nothing but flutter in the moment. The feeling of being loved and understood was overwhelming like a weighted blanket for his soul, and without thinking he leaned in, gently cradling Husk’s warm fuzzy face before kissing him. He noticed how Husk’s breath hitched, stiffening, before melting into the kiss. The warm buzz of love surrounded them and the world faded for a moment. Just them floating in the quiet intimacy of their embrace.
Angel finally pulled away, giggling at how some of his lipgloss was left behind on Husk’s lips. 
He used his big thumb to wipe it away, stopping for a second to memorize what his partner look like in this moment before asking, “Ready to go baby?” 
Husk chuckled deeply, before taking Angel’s hand to lead him out the door, without another word, clearly left speechless by the kiss.

“Dick?” Kory is not a woman who experiences shame or self-consciousness frequently. She is feeling both of these things now.
He looks up, greeting her with a smile. “Hey, what’s up, Kory?”
She doesn’t miss the way his eyes rove over her appreciatively. Normally, she would enjoy this. She loves looking beautiful. She loves looking beautiful for him.
She puts time and effort into her appearance; she likes it to be noticed.
But she doesn’t derive the same pleasure from his gaze today and she wraps her arms around herself.
Dick clocks the change instantly, his smile dropping. “What’s wrong, honey?”
“A man said something to me today,” she says. She sits carefully next to him and he scooches to make room for her. “About my outfit and about my… body.”Dick sits up a little straighter. “Oh?”“I thought he was complimenting me, but Donna explained to me what he meant.” She hugs her knees to her chest. “It was not a compliment.”
“What did he say to you?” Dick asks. He takes her hand in his, twining their fingers together. It’s comforting. She squeezes his hand back.
“I would rather not repeat it,” she says. Even thinking of it is enough to make her face warm. She doesn’t want Dick to know.“Alright.” Dick settles back, but Kory can see that his anger is only simmering. It hasn’t cooled.
“Is there something wrong with how I dress?” Kory blurts. It’s not something she ever worried about; how she chose to express herself isn’t something she’s ever needed anyone else’s validation on, but if she’s attracting that kind of attention… Maybe she should tone it down.
“What?” The question startles Dick. “Of course not! Look, Kory, some men are creeps. There’s no way around that.” He cups her face with his hands, pushing her hair away from her ears. “But you shouldn’t have to change how you act because of them. Sure, you’re going to attract attention, but that’s because you’re beautiful and kind, not because you did anything wrong.”
Kory smiles weakly. “I thought about blasting him with a starbolt.”
“Well, next time, maybe you should.”“Donna told me I shouldn’t.”He’s carding his fingers through her hair now. “Well… the starbolt would be more satisfying.”
Her smile becomes more sincere. “Yes.”

Whenever they make camp in a new place, Leya always stays up late organizing her collection of books.

 He
 pauses a moment, taken aback by this unexpected sight, but then he leaps to action.
 Or, rather, falls to his knees in action, wrapping his arms around the woman who owns his heart.
"Leya, what's wrong?" Gale asks.
Her body shudders before she turns to look at him.
 Her face is streaked with dirt and tears, and her hands shake as they find his.
"Sorry, sorry," she says, voice catching in her throat.
 "Sorry.""It's more than alright," Gale reassures her.
 "These are dark and difficult times, for you most of all.
 I'm happy to be a listening ear and a comforting pair of arms, if you wish."Leya smiles sadly at him.
 "You know how I collect all of these books and papers, right?"
"I have noticed that with my keen eye, yes," Gale says.
"I just... I did it for a reason.
 I know there was a reason.
 There was a face that I could remember.
 And the books are for him?
 But I can't remember him anymore," Leya says, voice tight in her throat.
 "I want to bring him the books.
 But now I can't remember his face or why I want to bring him the books.
 My mind is getting worse, not better.
 I'm... I can't forget more.
 What if I wake up and forget things since the tadpoles?
 What if I forget you?"
Gale's heart splits in two to see this woman he loves so much- who is always so certain, always so sure- suddenly so scared.
 He pulls her closer to him, pressing a kiss to the top of her head.
"I like to think I'm truly unforgettable."
 She gives a little shake of laughter at that, which heartens him.
 "But if you ever did wake up and forget me, then I would simply remind you of our adventures together.
 As many times as it took."
Leya smiles up at him.
 "And I would fall in love with you every single time."Gale meets her smile with one of his own.
 "You know... I've showed you things from my past with the tadpoles.
 If there's any memories you'd like preserved... I would love to be your repository."Leya covers her mouth with her hand and laughs softly before turning more serious.

 I know your hands as soft and gentle.

"Of course, my love," Gale replies.
They work quietly side by side, Gale admiring how the firelight bounces off of her scales.

 Somehow, miraculously, she likes just spending time with him.
He feels at ease in a way that's unfamiliar, in a way that makes him consider if what he had with Mystra was really what he thought it was.
A few nights later- after a particularly long day trudging through the shadowlands- he's woken up in the middle of the night.

 A memory, from before."The words shoot through him like lightning and he sits up.

“Plumbimg is þe hart of civilization.” (Sic, Ancient Plummings of þe Werld, pub. 1351)To plumb the depths of plumbing history is to plumb extremely deeply. The Temple of Bel in ancient Babylon captured rain and diverted waste with clay pipes, and Uruk, domain of the Half-blood wizard-king Gilgamesh, boasted of pipes to drain its latrines. In Europe, plumbing reached its antique height in the days of the Romans, who built a system of canals and sewers called the Cloaca Maxima, which carried away well nigh all the filth of that glorious city. Alas, upon the fall of the west wing of Rome in 476 so too fell the art of plumbing, which persisted only where it might be maintained and was expanded nowhere. For our purpose, with a sight fixed on the sanitary history of Britain, it is permissible to skip forward by half a millennium to Castle Hogwarts, where plumbing returned to our isle in the 10th century through the person of Salazar Slytherin.
The Founders of Hogwarts came from varied places and boasted varied backgrounds—and none was more varied in his personal history than that wizard surnamed Salazar. Records of his upbringing are scant¹ but historians agree that Salazar grew to adulthood somewhere upon the Spanish Peninsula, perhaps the Basque Country or Portugalia, well-positioned to become familiar with the sophisticated sewage systems of Moorish Spain.
By birthright or personal initiative, Salazar became a seafaring merchant and plied his trade from Norden to Constantinople—the anus of the Silk Road, for it was from this place that the fineries of the Far East were expelled into Europe—and in this course he attained a cosmopolitan wisdom that exceeded even that of Godric Gryffindor, who was born to a greater nobility but was less-travelled. It was not until he was fifty years old that Salazar turned his eyes to Britain, that country that would consume his attention and energy for the rest of his life.
We will not here retell the story of Hogwarts’ founding when so many other accounts are available. It will be sufficient to say that it is easy to overstate Salazar’s influence on Hogwarts, and incorrect to do so: while Hogwarts was doubtless influenced by Salazar’s knowledge of Islamic madrasas and the university of Constantinople, the school also owed a debt to the cathedral school of York, the palatial academy of Aix-la-Chapelle, and the uniquely British practice of dual monasteries. The result was unlike anything else in the world at that time, and nothing less than a collective project.
With this caveat out of the way, the original plumbing system at Hogwarts was certainly Salazar’s design alone, though the exact details were not recorded and so there is some uncertainty regarding its particulars. Some believe that Salazar installed the bathworks but that the inhabitants of Hogwarts Castle used latrines from the beginning; others say that he also installed toilets, but after Salazar departed there were none who could maintain the toilets, and so latrines replaced them.
Archaeological analysis of the original plumbing system at Hogwarts—such as still exists—suggests that Salazar took great inspiration from the designs laid forth in Op. Cit., the multidisciplinary masterwork of that famed Roman polymath, Ibid. The brightness was aggressive, invading the living room we had converted into a study bunker, exposing the grime, the smell of reheated coffee, and, worse, the stack of Law books that refused to make sense. He had fallen asleep on his open book, his head slumped at an awkward angle, his blonde hair falling over his forehead. The sight of that vulnerability was a physical blow. He looked like a child. The world exploded into vibrant color during the spring of Magpie’s sixth year, giving her many wonderful sights and smells to take in as she played in her cozy backyard.
 Intensely emerald eyes scanned the backyard as she searched for her favorite toys, struggling to remember where she had left them, half-knowing that they wouldn’t be there if her Fae friends had come over to play in the early morning hours without her.
 She stepped carefully, with flowered ankle-foot orthotics that rose to her mid-shin, held in place with neon pink straps, to support her weakened ankles.
 Magpie was born with a condition called hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome, a genetic condition that caused her connective tissue to be weaker and more pliable than the average person.
 She never seemed to notice that she was different than anyone her age because her peers tended to be of Fae origin.
 As she continued across the backyard, she noticed that the grass seemed to shimmer in the sunlight, some of the higher grass tickling her knees just below dark denim shorts.
 Squinting emerald eyes, she searched the backyard, knowing that when she saw this particular shimmer in the past, it typically meant that her Fae friends were near.
 “Daiya?
 Ember?
 Are you there?
 Eeva, don’t hide from me, it’s not fair!” Her soft voice hung in the humid air that surrounded the storybook cottage where she and her mother lived.
 It was the only home she’d ever known, yet there were times when it felt like a strange land.
 She dreamt of a faraway land that she’d never seen in the day, only in wild and vivid dreams that shook her awake.
 Magpie never really understood those dreams or why they were so important, but her Uncle Luke always asked to hear about them when her mom would tell him that she woke in the night crying again.
 Watching her young daughter in the backyard, Lauren’s rose-tinted lips curled upward into a smile before she turned away from the window, focusing her attention on the guests that had gathered in her kitchen.
 “Cecelia, what is the news from Pagawa?
 How is the catch looking for this season?”
 Lauren’s hazel eyes drifted from the small woman who had folded herself to be even smaller to the taller woman settled into the oversized armchair near the fireplace.
 “Melinda, how are the trades going?
 Will we be able to meet the demands of the Freyans?
 Last year, we barely met their demand, yet this year they want more.”
 Cecelia spoke first, her voice barely above a whisper from years of living on Pagawa where everyone used telepathic communication.
 Pagawa, a large island nation sheltered in the waters of the Pagalin Sea, thrived from fishing the deep, crystal-clear waters for various creatures, large and small.
 The island was nearly silent most of the time because the inhabitants developed telepathic communication to prevent the sea creatures from becoming spooked as their vessels trolled the waters.
 The only noise that was heard was the laughter of children who had not yet developed telepathic communication reliably.
 “The catch seems to be going well, but we need to increase our numbers if we are going to be able to survive the winter.”
 Raising a hand to silence Lauren before she could begin again, she continued, “Yes, yes, I know the winter is months away.
 In the last few years we have noticed that the numbers in our hauls have declined earlier and earlier in the year.
 Our scientists have been working on solutions, but it is tricky.
 We think that more are coming into our waters to fish without permission, but we haven’t been able to track them down just yet.”
 Lauren nodded, causing a piece of honey-hued hair to drift from the messy bun to her cheek.
 Her eyes danced over to the lanky woman curled into the oversized armchair, waiting for her to speak.
 “The Freyans demanded almost twice the amount of meat and fur that they were given last harvest, but our hunters can keep up with the demands.
 We have been branching out into new areas in the forest, finding larger species that allow us to meet the demands with less work.
 Our consultation with the Pagawali scientists tells us that these creatures are being driven out of the mountains surrounding Frey, but they do not know the reason.
 We hope that because the creatures are native to Frey that the Freyans will be more appeased by the meats and furs,” her voice rang out loudly in the quiet room, seeming to echo against the pale blue walls that were covered in a mixture of Magpie’s drawings and actual pictures of Magpie.

“I really meant it, you know? I really would like to get to know you. The real you, this time.”It was the kind of thing that Spamton would have never, not in a million years, imagined Tenna saying to him. To say the road to reconciliation had been a long one would be the understatement of the century, and perhaps even of the millenium. There were mountains of bitter memories to dig through, lies and manipulations and mis-directed cruelties. They’d beaten the shit out of each other and they’d screamed at each other and then they’d spent ages dancing around each other, talking in the stiff, stilted tones of actors that had forgotten to read the script until that morning. It had been about as messy as messy got.
Things got better slowly. There wasn’t really a clear moment where everything shifted from being ‘awful’ to being ‘maybe okay.’ It was just a gradual progression, the tremors slowly fading out of their voices and their movements becoming less and less stiff. They were in a… weird place, nowadays. There was a fragility to their relationship that hadn’t been there before, but just because things were ‘weird’ didn’t necessarily mean they were bad. Neither of them were exactly great at handling instability, but progress, Spamton supposed, was progress nonetheless.
And somehow, it had all led… here. Sitting outside Castle Town’s bakery on a bench too big for Spamton and too small for Tenna, watching the quiet falling of the first snow that winter. Warmth seeping into his fingers through the thick, fuzzy gloves he wore, courtesy of the hot chocolate Tenna had grabbed him from the Color Cafe. He found that he didn’t like coffee much these days, and he was past the point of being embarrassed about a more ‘childish’ drink choice. It helped that Tenna liked it too, even if the CRT’s wasn’t heated to near-boiling. It wasn’t like it was Spamton’s fault he ran cold these days.
He took another careful sip of his drink to avoid responding right away. If he was being semantic, Tenna’s statement hadn’t exactly been one that needed a response, by the strictest conversational rules. But it probably deserved something. And it definitely deserved something more put-together than whatever scrambled thoughts Spamton was going to spit out if he tried to respond without thinking first. Tenna waited patiently, albeit with that underlying current of nervousness that was his trademark.
It was a request that Spamton wasn’t entirely sure how he felt about. Guilty, maybe. He’d told Tenna as much as he could about his history. About his benefactor and the strings that had held him, about just how much of the Spamton that Tenna had once known had been a carefully constructed facade. The chains that still bound him, alterations to his code that lingered even after the connection was cut, didn’t let him explain everything as clearly as he’d like to, but he’d managed to explain enough for Tenna to fill in the pieces.He knew Tenna was conflicted about it. He could hardly blame the guy, he knew he’d be pretty pissed if he found out that a solid ninety percent, probably more, of what he knew about Tenna was just bullshit. How Tenna still wanted… anything to do with him after that was beyond him, and yet here they were. On a bench. Drinking hot chocolate. Together.
“Are you not saying anything because of what I said, or because it’s one of your bad days?” Tenna asked, prodding the silence as gently as he could. A long sigh whistled out through Spamton’s teeth as he set his cup back on his lap, trying to get some of the warmth to spread to his legs too. Even with most of his body bundled to high hell it was cold. He didn’t really produce natural body heat himself anymore, so there was only so much the layers could do.
“JUST… THINKING,” he said finally.
“What about?” Tenna asked. He shrugged haplessly, unsure how to even begin articulating the jumbled mess of thoughts currently rattling around his skull. He doubted it would make all that much sense if he tried to say it aloud. The wind picked up for a moment and he shivered at the cold, drawing in on himself in a feeble attempt at shielding himself.
“Cold?”“WHAT? OF [[Course]] NOT. CANT EV3N [Feel it],” Spamton said, his attempt at waving the concern off foiled by the way his voice shook as he spoke. Tenna rolled his antennae fondly, the unbroken one completing a full circuit while the other twitched weakly. He opened his arms in a wordless invitation. When Spamton didn’t object, an arm settled around his shoulders and pulled him flush against Tenna’s side. The warmth took a second to creep through the layers both of them were wearing, but Tenna was practically a furnace and it didn’t take long for the heat to envelop him from where Tenna held him.
“Better?” Tenna asked, voice teasing. Spamton snorted, but the desire to appear unbothered wasn’t enough to stop him from pressing in closer. It really was better. He felt more than he heard Tenna’s resulting laugh. “Do you want to go back inside?”
